Where does Beavercreek fit in the Dayton area?

Beavercreek is the largest city in Greene County and lies about five miles east of downtown Dayton, so many of its homes sit within a short drive of Dayton jobs. Census estimates put the city at 48,134 residents for 2025, spread over about 26.6 square miles of land.

Settlers arrived in the early 1800s, and part of Beavercreek Township incorporated as a city in February 1980. The city absorbed the former communities of Alpha, Knollwood, most of New Germany and Zimmerman, and an older deed may use one of those names. The legal description and parcel number in your deed matter more to a title company than the neighborhood label.

Growth has been gradual. Wikipedia's census table lists 37,984 residents in 2000, 45,193 in 2010 and 46,549 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 48,134 is about 3% above the 2020 base. A mayor elected directly by voters and six at-large council members run the city, with a city manager appointed by council, and public meetings air on the city's cable channel.

How do Beavercreek housing numbers compare with Lorain County suburbs?

Beavercreek has a larger renter share than Avon Lake or Avon. In the 2020 to 2024 data, 71.8% of homes are owner-occupied, the median home value is $279,600 and the median rent is $1,457. The city has 19,453 households averaging 2.39 people, and monthly owner costs are $1,837 with a mortgage and $838 without.

  • The 2020 census counted 19,980 housing units, 5.3% of them vacant.
  • Among occupied units, 72.6% were owner-occupied and 27.4% rented.
  • The median age was 40.6, and 20.0% of residents were 65 or older.

More than a quarter of occupied homes are rented, so landlords and renters make up part of the demand. A homeowner with a long repair list can ask a direct buyer about an as-is purchase instead of renovating first.

Which Beavercreek permits and registrations come up at sale?

Permits split between the city and the county. The city's Planning and Development Department issues zoning permits, and Greene County Building Regulation handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits. The table lists the permit the city names for common projects, which helps you spot open work before a buyer's inspector does.

Permit that Beavercreek lists for common residential projects
ProjectPermit or office
New house, addition or attached garageResidential Zoning Permit
DeckResidential Zoning Permit
Swimming poolSwimming Pool Permit
Shed or detached garage, propane tankAccessory Structure Permit
Fence or retaining wallFence Permit
Interior remodel such as wall removal or a finished basementGreene County Building Regulation, no zoning permit
Abandoned, foreclosure or vacant propertyRegistration Application

Sources: beavercreekohio.gov.

Zoning permits are not required for interior remodeling, at-grade patios, garage sales or driveways. Applications run through the online permit center, and printed forms can be filed at City Hall on Research Park Drive. If the house is vacant, ask the planning office whether the registration rule applies to it.

  • Greene County Building Regulation, at 667 Dayton-Xenia Road in Xenia, issues building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.
  • Greene County Public Health, at 360 Wilson Drive in Xenia, is the county contact for health department questions.
  • Greene County Sanitary Engineering, at the same Dayton-Xenia Road address, is the contact for sewer questions.
  • The Beavercreek Fire Department is at 851 N. Orchard Lane.

Are short-term rentals allowed in Beavercreek?

They are, with a city license. Ordinance 23-15 and Chapter 117 of the city code require every owner to apply through the Online Permit Center before renting for fewer than thirty consecutive days. A license lasts two years and must be renewed.

  • The application lists the location, where the unit will be advertised, bedrooms, maximum occupants, parking and emergency contacts.
  • Renters must be at least 25 years old, and owners must hand them house rules, noise rules and emergency details.
  • The city's 3% hotel, motel and short-term rental tax is filed quarterly, even for quarters with no rentals.

Owners inside a homeowners association should read its covenants first, as the city advises. For a house that has run as a rental, tell buyers about the license and the tax filings, and ask the planning office whether a new owner must file a fresh application.

How does Greene County process a Beavercreek deed?

The Greene County Auditor transfers the deed, and the recorder files it afterward. The auditor requires a completed Real Property Conveyance Statement of Value and Receipt (form DTE 100), and the grantor's name must match how the grantor took title in the previous deed. The county map department must approve the deed before it reaches the auditor, and land in the farmland tax program needs the DTE 101 statement.

The auditor's page prints the cost this way: a transfer tax of fifty cents per parcel and a conveyance fee of $2 for every thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county offers an online calculator. The recorder's standards add a complete legal description with the parcel number, a prepared-by statement, the prior deed reference and a notarial acknowledgment.

How are Greene County property taxes handled for a sale?

The county auditor appraises each parcel at fair market value every six years and updates values every three. The auditor's office is at 69 Greene Street in Xenia, and its appraisers will talk through a valuation or start an appeal. Property taxes fund schools, public safety, roads, libraries and parks.

Due dates move with state changes. For the second half of 2026, the Greene County Treasurer announced that the House Bill 186 inflation cap credit delayed bills, and that the Tax Commissioner approved a payment due date of Friday, August 14, 2026. Escrow borrowers had no action to take. For your own closing year, ask the treasurer for the schedule and have the title company prorate the tax between you and the buyer.

What do Beavercreek schools, parks and transit mean for buyers?

Beavercreek City School District has one preschool, six elementary schools, two middle schools, a Freshman School and Beavercreek High School. The parks department maintains 24 parks and properties, and Beavercreek Station is a hub on Creekside Trail, which runs from Xenia to Eastwood MetroPark in Dayton. The Greater Dayton Regional Transit Authority runs bus service in the city, and the public library is a branch of the Greene County Public Library.

These details help a listing, and they also tell a direct buyer what the house is worth to the next owner. If you sell as is, ask the buyer to state in writing that repairs are theirs, and keep a copy of any inspection report you ordered.

More questions about Beavercreek, OH

Do I need a city permit to sell a house in Beavercreek?

The city's permit list covers construction work, short-term rental licenses and registration of vacant or foreclosure properties. Check for open permits on past work, since decks, pools, fences and sheds need zoning permits and the county handles building, plumbing, electrical and HVAC permits.

What fees does Greene County charge on a deed?

The auditor's page lists a transfer tax of fifty cents per parcel and a conveyance fee of $2 per thousand dollars of the sale price, rounded up to the nearest $100. The county's online calculator shows the amount for your sale.

Can a Beavercreek short-term rental license pass to a buyer?

Ask the planning office. Licenses last two years and go to the owner who applies, so a new owner may need to file a new application through the Online Permit Center.

When are Greene County taxes due?

Dates are set each year. The second half of 2026 was due Friday, August 14, 2026, after a delay tied to House Bill 186. Ask the Greene County Treasurer for the schedule that matches your closing.

What must I disclose when I sell my Beavercreek home?

Complete the Ohio property disclosure form if the home has up to four units. ORC 5302.30 lists exceptions such as estate sales and transfers to relatives, and the signed deed must be acknowledged before a notary under ORC 5301.01.

What must a Euclid owner do before agreeing to sell?

A Euclid owner must obtain a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance from the Housing Department before entering into a sale agreement, then hand the certificate to the buyer. Chapter 1759 of the city's codified ordinances makes it unlawful to agree to sell or convey a dwelling without that certificate in hand.

The rule is the single biggest difference between selling here and in most Ohio suburbs, so plan around it from day one. A city inspector goes through the house and the lot after you buy the application, and the resulting list of known violations guides your next steps: fix the items, or let the buyer take them on.

How do Euclid's Point of Sale terms work?

The ordinance sets the terms in plain numbers, and they are the same for every seller. Here is how Chapter 1759 reads.

Euclid Point of Sale rules, Codified Ordinances Chapter 1759
ItemWhat the ordinance says
Application fee$225.00, plus $35.00 per unit for buildings with more than three units
Life of the certificateSix months, and no new inspection if the property sells in that period
Renewal after no sale50% of the original fee, if the owner reports in writing within 30 days after expiration
Elderly owners with the county homestead exemptionFee drops to $100.00, except for transfers caused by the owner's death
Violations still open at saleBuyer files an Assumption application and corrects them within 180 days of transfer
Sheriff's sale purchase of a one, two or three family homeBuyer purchases the application within ten days, corrects violations within 180 days

Owners of one or two family homes who sell and relocate within Euclid can apply for a rebate of the $225.00 fee when they buy another one or two family residence as their primary home. Assumed violations that stay open past 180 days can lead to prosecution under Section 1703.99.

Who answers questions at Euclid's Building and Housing office?

The Building, Housing and Nuisance Department takes calls Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at (216) 289-2700. Extension 3908 covers Point of Sale and assumptions, 3904 residential permits, 3905 rental requirements, 3906 tall grass and yard debris, and 3903 vacant property registration. Permit applications go by email to buildingandhousing@cityofeuclid.gov as attachments, since the office cannot accept photos of forms.

  • Ask about the Point of Sale inspection before you list so the violation list is in your hands when buyers call.
  • Ask whether a vacant house must be registered with the city, because Chapter 1763 ties exemptions to a current Point of Sale inspection and a for sale status.
  • Fence and shed questions go to the same office. The city caps combined garage and shed area at 696 square feet and allows no shed taller than ten feet.

The city's Housing Accessibility and Rehabilitation Grant Program excludes problems found in a Point of Sale inspection, and the city reported that all 2026 grant funds were committed by early October. Do not count on that grant to pay for sale repairs.

What is it like to own a house in Euclid?

Euclid sits on the southern shore of Lake Erie as an inner ring suburb of Cleveland, in Cuyahoga County, and borders Cleveland to the west, South Euclid and Richmond Heights to the south and Willowick, Wickliffe and Willoughby Hills to the east. It covers 11.48 square miles, about 10.63 of them land. The city is part of the Lake Erie Snowbelt, so snow squalls off the lake test roofs, gutters and driveways every winter, and buyers look at those items closely.

Euclid Village was incorporated in 1903 and became a city in 1930. Population jumped from 12,751 in 1930 to 41,396 in 1950 and peaked at 71,552 in 1970, so the city grew fastest in the 1940s and 1950s. The 1926 U.S. Supreme Court case Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. opened the door for zoning ordinances across the country, and Lincoln Electric still has its main plant and headquarters here. Charles Brush produced the arc lamp in Euclid in 1876, and in June 2011 Lincoln Electric raised a 2.5 megawatt wind turbine, 443 feet tall and listed as the largest in Ohio.

The city counted 49,692 people in 2020, making it the fourth largest city in Cuyahoga County, at 4,663.7 residents per square mile. Elevation is about 617 feet, a beachfront runs along the north edge, and mail uses ZIP codes 44117, 44119, 44123, 44132 and 44143 under area code 216. The Euclid Public Library and the Euclid Heritage Trail project add to the amenities buyers ask about.

Euclid City Schools is the public school district, with Euclid High School as its high school. In late October 2026 the city posted a notice about the Cleveland Water Division's Lead Service Line Replacement Program, so ask the water division whether work is planned at your address.

What do Census figures show for Euclid housing?

Census Bureau QuickFacts lists Euclid's July 2025 population at 47,962, down 3.5 percent from the April 2020 base. Fewer than half of homes are lived in by their owners, at 46.4 percent for 2020 to 2024.

  • Median value of an owner occupied home: $126,500
  • Median gross rent: $1,025
  • Households: 22,433, averaging 2.16 people
  • Median household income: $50,285
  • Persons in poverty: 16.6 percent
  • Average commute: 25.9 minutes
  • Adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or higher: 23.2 percent

The gap between rent at $1,025 and owner values at $126,500 is the number rental buyers study. A rental owner who sells should know that Ohio Revised Code 5323.02 requires owners of residential rental property to file ownership details with the county Fiscal Officer.

How does the deed move through Cuyahoga County?

The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division, at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland, phone 216-443-2060, handles the deed. Every transfer needs either a DTE 100 Statement of Value and Receipt or a DTE 100-EX exemption form. Office hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with recording until 4:00 p.m.

The standard recording fee is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after, a change that took effect October 24, 2024 under Ohio Senate Bill 94. The county reminds owners that preparing a deed counts as the practice of law, and county staff cannot advise on it, so a title company or attorney normally drafts it.

The city's inspection is a separate matter from state law. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 also asks sellers of one to four unit homes to deliver a signed property disclosure form to buyers, so a Euclid seller usually completes both the state form and the city's Point of Sale paperwork.

More questions about Euclid, OH

Does Euclid require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. Chapter 1759 requires a Point of Sale application and a Certificate of Code Compliance before you agree to sell, and the buyer must receive a copy. The application fee is $225.00.

What if my Euclid house fails the Point of Sale inspection?

You can fix the violations, or the buyer can take them on by filing an Assumption application and correcting them within 180 days of the transfer. Call extension 3908 at (216) 289-2700 for the steps.

How long does a Euclid Certificate of Code Compliance last?

It lasts six months. If the property sells during that period, no new Point of Sale inspection is required for the sale.

Can a senior pay less for the Euclid Point of Sale application?

Yes. The fee falls to $100.00 for elderly Euclid homeowners who receive the Cuyahoga County homestead exemption, except when the property transfers because the owner died.

Where is a Euclid deed filed?

The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office Transfer and Recording division in Cleveland receives it with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form. Call 216-443-2060 to confirm what your document needs.

How does Mansfield's housing market compare on the numbers?

Mansfield posts the lowest median rent and the smallest households of the four Ohio cities the Census Bureau compares here. Owners live in 50.5 percent of its homes, and 19.9 percent of residents are 65 or older.

Mansfield statisticResult

People per household2.13

Median gross rent$814
Median household income$44,540
Share aged 65 or older19.9%

Every row comes from the Census QuickFacts comparison. Headcount is nearly flat, down 0.2 percent from the 2020 estimates base.

What is Mansfield's location and early history?

Mansfield stands about halfway between Cleveland and Columbus along Interstate 71, in the western foothills of the Allegheny Plateau. The land is hilly: Central Park downtown stands near 1,240 feet, and the city's high point of 1,493 feet is a water reservoir off Woodland Road in the southwest.

Surveyors laid out the town in June 1808 around a public square beside a fork of the Mohican River and named it for the federal Surveyor General who directed the plan. The village charter came in 1828 and the city charter in 1857. Rail service began with a line in 1846, and by the late 1880s four railroads had turned Mansfield into a trading and manufacturing center.

The Lincoln Highway reached Mansfield in 1913 along what is now Park Avenue East and West, which became U.S. Route 30 in 1928.

What happened to Mansfield's factories?

Mansfield made tires, stoves, brass goods and appliances, and then lost most of that work. In the late 1950s Westinghouse alone had over 8,000 workers here, and the Mansfield Tire and Rubber Company closed in 1979, leaving 1,721 workers without jobs.

The steel recession of the 1970s, overseas competition, long labor disputes and aging plants led most heavy industry to leave, with the AK Steel Mansfield Works as the last large survivor. The city was placed in fiscal emergency by the state auditor in 2010 and released on July 9, 2014. Big-box retail shifted to the suburb of Ontario, which replaced Mansfield as the county's shopping center.

What remains includes Therm-O-Disc, The Gorman-Rupp Company, Ideal Electric, The Carousel Works and a service sector built on health care and education. Census figures for 2022 show health care and social assistance receipts of $650.7 million, with transportation and warehousing at $191.5 million.

Which roads, schools and colleges serve Mansfield?

Interstate 71 reaches Mansfield through three exits, giving access to Cleveland in one direction and Columbus in the other. The Martin Luther King Jr. Freeway, which is U.S. 30, is the one limited-access road inside the city and heads toward Bucyrus in the west and Wooster in the east. Ohio 13 and Ohio 309 are divided highways, and U.S. 42 is a major arterial.

Mansfield City Schools operate eight schools, including a Spanish immersion school, and the Madison Local School District covers the eastern parts of the city. Higher education comes from The Ohio State University at Mansfield, North Central State College and an Ashland University nursing building on Trimble Road.

Since two districts reach into the city, a seller should confirm the right one for the address before it goes in a listing.

What do Mansfield winters mean for an older house?

Lake Erie lies 38 miles north, and its influence helps push snowfall to an average of 49.2 inches a season, lighter than the snowbelt to the northeast. Mean temperature in January is 26.5 degrees Fahrenheit, with about five days a year at or below zero.

The record 24-hour snowfall, 23 inches on December 22 and 23, 2004, arrived during a major ice storm. Buyers who know that history may ask about roof age, insulation, sump pumps and the furnace, so keep receipts for work done on them.

How does a deed move through the Richland County offices?

Richland County accepts electronic deed transfers, and the recorder's page says each deed must include tax map pre-approval. Documents that need tax map or auditor review have to be delivered in person to the courthouse.

The recorder and the auditor both work from 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. Recording of documents ends at 3:45 p.m., and the office states that it supplies no legal forms and urges people to ask an attorney for guidance.

  • Request tax map pre-approval first.
  • Carry any auditor-reviewed paperwork to the courthouse in person.
  • Leave the legal description to an attorney or title company.

Who can witness a Mansfield seller's signature?

A deed must be signed and acknowledged under section 5301.01. The statute names the officials who may certify the acknowledgment: judges and court clerks, county auditors and engineers, notaries and mayors.

A bank branch, a title office or a county office with a notary is the usual stop. Bring photo identification and avoid signing ahead of time, since the official must witness the act of acknowledging.

What can a buyer find downtown in Mansfield?

Mansfield calls itself the Carousel Capital of Ohio and carries the official nickname The Fun Center of Ohio. Downtown revolves around the public square that surveyors drew in 1808, now called Central Park, and the 1929 relocation of a War of 1812 blockhouse to South Park.

Downtown Mansfield, Inc., formerly Main Street Mansfield, works on revitalization, and the Mansfield/Richland County Public Library has served the area since 1887 with nine branches. These details help a listing describe the setting beyond the house itself.

What building and zoning help does the city offer?

Building and Codes works from the third floor at 30 North Diamond Street. Its Citizen Access Portal accepts permit requests and contractor registrations around the clock, while the front desk is staffed from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays except federal holidays and the day after Thanksgiving.

The page links a zoning map with layers for addresses, utilities, flood plain and contours, a summary of what needs a permit, and Planning Commission schedules. Plumbing inspections go through the Richland County Health Department. If you plan repairs before selling, check whether the work needs a permit, because unpermitted work can surface at an inspection.

More questions about Mansfield, OH

Can I sell a Mansfield house that needs major repairs?

Yes. Nothing in Ohio law requires repairs before a sale. Price it to reflect the work, or sell to a buyer who pays cash and plans to renovate.

Where do I take a deed in Mansfield?

Ask Richland County for tax map pre-approval first, then go through the auditor and recorder at 50 Park Avenue East. E-filed transfers are accepted, yet paperwork that needs tax map and auditor review has to come in person.

Who can notarize my deed in Mansfield?

A judge, clerk of a court of record, county auditor, county engineer, notary public or mayor can take the acknowledgment under section 5301.01. A notary at a bank or title office is the easiest choice.

Is a Mansfield house in the Madison school district?

Possibly. Madison Local serves eastern parts of Mansfield, while Mansfield City Schools cover the rest. Check the county auditor's parcel record or ask the district about the specific address.

Does Mansfield require permits for repairs before I sell?

Many repairs do. The city's Building and Codes department accepts permit requests online at any hour and publishes a guide on what needs a permit. Plumbing inspections go through the Richland County Health Department.

What does a Mentor seller need to line up first?

Mentor is a Lake Erie suburb northeast of Cleveland with more people than any other Lake County city. Painesville is where the county auditor takes deeds. Back in Mentor, city codes on lawns, permits, curbside bins and walks are the sort of thing a buyer's agent may mention.

The April 2020 census found 47,450 residents, and the 2025 estimate of 47,010 is a shade lower. A Mentor seller mostly faces other single-family listings, so condition, paperwork and timing carry real weight. What follows covers local numbers, city rules, county filings and the cases where a direct cash sale deserves a look.

What do Census figures say about Mentor homeowners and prices?

About 85 of every 100 Mentor households own where they live. The midpoint for an owned home is far above those for Middletown or Newark, so repairs and presentation matter more here.

Nearly a quarter of residents are 65 or older, and the median age at the 2020 census was 48.0. A seller in that age mix may be moving to a smaller place, closing out a parent's estate or heading toward family, and a move like that often has a firm date.

Where did Mentor's housing come from?

Charles Parker built the first settlement in 1797. Settlers from the Connecticut Western Reserve named the town for a Greek classical figure, as they did with several neighbors. James A. Garfield bought a home here in 1876 and ran his 1880 presidential campaign from the porch. The property is now the James A. Garfield National Historic Site.

Census counts leapt from 4,354 in 1960 to 36,912 in 1970, which suggests a large share of today's houses were built close together in time. Homes from a boom like that may still carry original roofs, older electrical panels and finished basements, all of which inspectors test hard.

Lake Erie weather adds wear. Annual precipitation averages about 42.87 inches, with more than 93 days a year that bring over a tenth of an inch of rain. Check gutters, downspouts, grading and sump pumps before you list, since basement water is one of the first subjects a buyer raises.

Which Mentor city rules apply to a seller?

The city's resident pages and FAQ spell out the rules. These items come up most while a house is readied for market:

  • Permits. Decks, pools, siding, sheds, porches and enclosures all need one. Sort out unpermitted work with the Engineering and Building Department early.
  • High grass. Growth averaging over eight inches is rank vegetation. Code Enforcement posts the house, the owner gets 48 hours, and after that Public Works mows and sends a bill.
  • House numbers. Numerals need a four inch minimum height, and houses set well back from the road need larger ones.
  • Trash bins. Containers may go to the tree lawn after 7 in the evening before pickup and must be gone from it by 7 that evening.
  • Sidewalks. The owner maintains the walk that runs through the public right-of-way.
  • Sewer trouble. Lake County Utilities checks the main line. If the main works, the lateral is the owner's problem.

Mentor is a NOPEC energy-aggregation community, and water, sewer and trash each come from a different provider, so list all three contacts in the buyer's packet. Before signing a purchase contract, ask Code Enforcement if any notice is open on your address.

How does Lake County record a Mentor sale?

Before the Lake County Auditor endorses a deed, someone for the buyer must file DTE 100 with the price, or DTE 100EX if an exemption applies. Sellers who held the homestead reduction also file DTE 101, and those with farmland on agricultural valuation file DTE 102.

Expect $4.00 for every $1,000 of the sale price, rounded up to a full hundred, and an added $.50 per parcel. The auditor's FAQ says $1.00 of that goes to the state and $3.00 to the county. Sellers pay when the deed is presented, on a check apart from recording charges.

  • A conveyance of part of a lot, or any metes and bounds description, needs prior approval from the Lake County Engineer's tax map office.
  • Find the auditor at 105 Main Street, Suite C101, in Painesville, open weekdays from 8:00 until 4:30.
  • Either party, or a representative, may submit the deed, and the office takes it by mail.
  • The signer acknowledges the deed before a notary or an official listed in R.C. 5301.01.

The auditor advises that an attorney or title company draw up the papers.

How is property tax handled when a Mentor house sells?

Bills from Lake County go out around mid-January and mid-June, with payment expected roughly 20 to 30 days later. The treasurer collects, and the title company splits the year so each party pays for its months of ownership.

One useful point from the auditor's FAQ: only the assessed value can be challenged, since voters approve the levies behind the rate. Value complaints go to the Board of Revision. Ohio law (R.C. 319.202) also has the buyer ask whether the house received a homestead or similar tax reduction last year or this year, which tells both sides how the first bill under the new owner could shift.

Must a Mentor seller give the buyer a disclosure form?

R.C. 5302.30 covers homes of one to four units. The owner completes the state form, which asks about water supply, sewage, roof, foundation, walls, floors, hazardous materials and known defects, then gets a signed copy to every prospective buyer promptly.

Delivering it before an offer exists keeps things simple. When it arrives afterward, the buyer can withdraw in writing within three business days of receipt, and the window shuts at day 30 after acceptance or at closing if sooner. Estate fiduciaries and heirs who have not lived in the house for a year are excused.

When is a cash sale a good fit for a Mentor house?

A direct sale can work when speed outweighs price. Think of a house inherited with a full attic, a home with a worn roof or damp basement, a property with code notices, or an owner who relocated.

Hold any offer up against what a listing would leave in your pocket after repairs, closing charges and months of carrying costs. Ask who pays the Lake County conveyance charge, how quickly the closing can happen and whether the price can move after the buyer's walkthrough. Sign a contract and close through a title company or lawyer.

More questions about Mentor, OH

Do I have to hire a lawyer to sell in Mentor?

No state rule requires it. The county auditor does recommend a lawyer or title agent for the deed and transfer forms, and acknowledgment follows R.C. 5301.01.

What is the Lake County transfer charge?

Its page prints $4.00 per $1,000 of price, price rounded up by the hundred, plus $.50 per parcel, paid by the seller. Verify with the auditor before closing.

Can a Mentor house with a code notice still sell?

Yes, though you should clear it or disclose it. Ask Code Enforcement or Engineering and Building where your address stands. Unpermitted work can slow an inspection or draw a lower offer.

What is the typical value of a Mentor home?

QuickFacts reports a midpoint of $247,700. Half of Mentor's owned homes are worth more and half less, so yours could land on either side depending on size, age and upkeep.

How is property tax split between a Mentor seller and buyer?

The purchase contract and closing statement settle it, and the title company usually prorates each party's share of the January and June bills. Read that line before you sign.

What is it like to sell a house in Delaware, Ohio?

Whether a Delaware owner hires an agent, goes it alone, or deals with a cash buyer, the deed ends up with the Delaware County Auditor and Recorder. The city is the county seat, set on the Olentangy River along U.S. Route 23 north of Columbus. Growth has been fast: the Census Bureau puts July 2025 at 46,636 people, 12.9 percent above its 2020 base of 41,297.

The city's own fast-facts page says Delaware draws people looking for affordability, lower income taxes, good schools and small town living. It also says the population has almost doubled since 2000.

Why does Delaware's history show up in its housing?

Delaware is an older town, and the oldest streets sit around downtown and the university. The city was built on the site of a Mingo village called Pluggy's Town, and the town plan was filed in 1808. In 1812, Delaware lost the vote to become Ohio's capital by a single vote to Columbus.

Railroads arrived in 1851, and Ohio Wesleyan University was founded in 1844. The university still anchors downtown along South Sandusky Street, and the city says its downtown is 94 percent occupied.

How do Delaware's homeowner statistics read?

Census Bureau QuickFacts for 2020 through 2024 describe Delaware this way:

  • Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $318,400, and 64.7 percent of the 16,728 households own.
  • Households average 2.57 people; renters pay a median gross rent of $1,286.
  • Owners with a mortgage have median monthly costs of $1,892.
  • Median household income is $99,786, and 47.8 percent of adults 25 and over hold at least a bachelor's degree.
  • Workers spend 25.6 minutes getting to work on average.
  • Residents under 18 make up 23.8 percent, and those 65 and older 14.7 percent.

Which public schools cover a Delaware address?

Three public districts reach into the city, so one block can differ from the next. The city's fast-facts page sizes each one.

The Delaware City district's high school is Rutherford B. Hayes High School, and its middle school is John C. Dempsey Middle School. Check the parcel before a listing names a district.

What roads and employers tie Delaware to the region?

U.S. Routes 23, 36 and 42 pass through the city, and Ohio Route 37 crosses it east to west. The Delaware Municipal Airport lies southwest of the central business district.

The city says no single sector dominates its economy. Its top employers include Kroger grocery and distribution at about 2,496 jobs, Ohio Wesleyan University at 1,571, Delaware County government at 1,114, OhioHealth at 1,022 and Delaware City Schools at 996. The list also includes automotive parts distribution, manufacturing and health care. The same page says many local graduates rent for a time and buy once they have families.

What do parks and downtown add to a Delaware listing?

The city lists three larger community parks, a public swimming pool, miles of trails, an executive golf course, two free splash pads and an urban forest of more than 18,000 trees. The Delaware Community Center YMCA is another named amenity. Downtown has about 310,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial space, around 60 percent of it retail, restaurant and entertainment use.

Those are concrete points to put in a listing. The city also reports bronze-level SolSmart status from 2022, a small solar array at its public works facility and a conversion of streetlights to LED.

Which city permit and property rules touch a Delaware sale?

One city department handles zoning, property maintenance and building review, and its building division is state-certified. Its FAQ answers several questions a seller or buyer will hit.

  • Structural, electrical or mechanical work likely needs a permit; so do fences, decks, sheds, garages and additions. Patios do not.
  • Property line disputes are a civil matter between neighbors; the city suggests having the parcel surveyed.
  • Starting in 2026, contractors no longer need to register with the city.
  • All vehicles, including trailers, must be parked on a hard surface such as asphalt, concrete or existing gravel; new or expanded gravel parking is not allowed.
  • Signs in the right-of-way, tree lawns and on utility poles are prohibited and are removed by code enforcement.

Formal violation notices are posted on the property, and a vacant property's notice is mailed to the owner of record with the county auditor. When a deadline passes, the city may make the fix and invoice the owner, and unpaid invoices can turn into a lien or ride on the tax bill. Charges through the city prosecutor are also possible. Clear any notice before listing, because a lien shows up in a title search.

What do the Delaware County offices handle on valuation, deeds and recording?

The Delaware County Auditor's page on the 2026 triennial update says the informal review period is over. A formal complaint about a valuation goes to the Board of Revision, with filing open from January 1, 2027, through March 31, 2027, on the form listed with the Auditor's other forms. That page also carries the Real Property Conveyance Fee Statement, DTE 100, and the Auditor's office can quote the conveyance fee rate for your sale.

Recording follows. The Recorder's fee page shows $39 for a deed's first two pages, a figure that includes a $5 preservation surcharge, plus $8 for every added page. The office sits at 145 N. Union Street and accepts documents until 4:00 p.m. on weekdays, with recordings handled between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. Rates on a county page can change, so call before mailing a check.

What does the state require a Delaware seller to disclose?

Under R.C. 5302.30, an owner of a home with up to four units must complete the Ohio disclosure form and give the buyer a signed copy. A buyer who sees the form, or a later amendment, only after signing may cancel in writing within three business days, as long as that happens before the earlier of thirty days from acceptance and closing.

The rule reaches sales, land installment contracts, lease-options and exchanges. Heirs who have not lived in an inherited house for a year are excluded, and so are transfers between spouses or to direct-line relatives.

When does a cash purchase help a Delaware owner?

A cash purchase helps when time or condition outweighs the last dollar of price. Deferred repairs, a code notice, sitting tenants or an unsettled estate can slow a listing. A buyer taking the house as it is removes showings and repair haggling.

Weigh any figure against a listed sale after repairs, the months of carrying costs, and the property tax still accruing. Keep each buyer's written price, closing date and cost split side by side.

More questions about Delaware, OH

What is the window to contest a Delaware County valuation?

The 2026 triennial update's informal review has closed. The Auditor lists a formal complaint to the Board of Revision as open from January 1, 2027, to March 31, 2027, using the Auditor's own form.

Which home projects need a Delaware permit?

Fences, decks, sheds, garages and home additions need permits, and so does any structural, electrical or mechanical work. Patios do not. Ask the Building Division what is needed to close an unpermitted structure before listing.

What if I ignore a Delaware violation notice?

The city can fix the problem and bill you, and an unpaid bill may become a lien or join your property tax bill. It can also recommend charges through the city prosecutor.

Where is the Delaware County Recorder and what are its deed fees?

The Recorder's office is at 145 N. Union Street in Delaware. Its fee page shows $39 for the first two pages, with a $5 preservation surcharge built in, and $8 per added page.

How do I tell which district my Delaware home is in?

It might be Delaware City, Olentangy Local or Buckeye Valley, since all three reach into the city. Match the parcel with county records or the district before naming one.

Selling in Strongsville?

Should a Strongsville owner list the house or take a cash offer?

Timing and condition decide it. An updated Strongsville house suits the open market, while one with deferred work or an estate attached may sell faster to a buyer who asks for no repairs. Owners occupy 82 percent of the homes, so many sellers are leaving a place they have held for years.

  • Agent listing: exposure to Cleveland-area buyers, with inspection and appraisal hurdles still ahead.
  • Owner-run sale: no commission, but the pricing, contract and disclosure form are yours to handle.
  • As-is cash purchase: one negotiation, no staging, and a closing date set by agreement.

Each path finishes with a deed presented to the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, so ask a title company or attorney to prepare the deed and the conveyance form before you accept an offer.

What should a seller know about Strongsville?

Strongsville is a Cleveland suburb of 24.64 square miles in Cuyahoga County. The name honors John Stoughton Strong, who brought settlers here in 1816, and the township was officially organized on February 25, 1818. Village status came in 1923, followed by city status in 1961.

The city's nickname, Crossroads of the Nation, began where a railroad met an electric line between Cleveland and Wooster. Since that line closed in 1931 the motto and seal point to Interstate 71 and the Ohio Turnpike instead. Highway access can headline a listing.

The Rocky River's east branch enters Strongsville from North Royalton and leaves toward Berea, and Cleveland Metroparks manage its banks as Mill Stream Run Reservation, with Bonnie Park and Ranger Lake. GCRTA buses run through town. Southpark Mall and the Strongsville Business and Technology Park, described as the largest industrial park in Northeast Ohio, are two of its major commercial sites. The Pomeroy House, built in 1847, was a stop on the Underground Railroad, and Beebetown is a historic neighborhood.

How does Census data describe Strongsville homeowners?

Strongsville's 2025 estimate is 45,629 people, which is 1.8 percent under its 2020 base. The rows below give the backdrop for pricing talks.

Strongsville city, Ohio. Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts (estimate July 1, 2025; remaining rows 2020-2024)

Who lives in Strongsville, and who buys there?

In 2020 the median age here was 45.8, and 22.9 percent of residents were 65 or older. Married couples headed 58.2 percent of the 18,643 households, while 26.0 percent were people living alone. Vacancy touched 3.9 percent of the 19,406 housing units.

That points to many long-term owners. When one downsizes or an estate settles, a dated kitchen, bath or furnace can be easier to sell around than to renovate. About 48.3 percent of adults have at least a bachelor's degree, and workers spend 25.5 minutes getting to work on average. Median household income is $103,253, 5.3 percent of residents live in poverty, and 10.4 percent were born outside the United States. Owners without a mortgage report median monthly costs of $822, compared with $1,935 for those who still carry one, so a paid-off house changes what the owner needs from a sale.

Which Strongsville schools and parks matter to buyers?

Strongsville City Schools has five elementary buildings (Chapman, Kinsner, Muraski, Surrarrer and Whitney), a middle school on Pearl Road and a high school on Lunn Road. Allen, Drake and Zellers elementary schools have closed as enrollment fell. St. Joseph and John's is a Catholic school through eighth grade.

A bond issue of $81 million passed in 2012 and paid for a combined middle school, high school renovations and technology upgrades, with the new middle school ready for 2016-2017.

  • Town Center Park, opened in 2024 with a pavilion, two playgrounds, and tennis, pickleball and volleyball courts.
  • Ehrnfelt Recreation and Senior Center, the Walter F. Ehrnfelt Covered Bridge and the Strongsville ice rink.
  • Strongsville Commons and the Clock Tower, site of the Homecoming and the Rib Burnoff.
  • Gardenview Horticultural Park and the Freedom Trail veterans memorial.

Community events cluster around the Commons and the Clock Tower: the Homecoming, the Rib Burnoff, a Winter Lighting Ceremony and, each September, the Harvest Festival at the Historical Society's village of restored buildings and a replica log cabin. A house near Town Center Park or the Commons can say so in its listing.

What does the Strongsville Building Department handle?

Permits, contractor registration, business licensing, inspections and code compliance all run through the office at 16099 Foltz Parkway. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, online submissions are accepted at any time, and the phone is 440-580-3105.

The city lists additions, decks, fences, sheds, roofs, windows and doors, pools, electrical, plumbing, HVAC and garages as permit work. A contractor has to register with Strongsville before a permit can be issued, and a homeowner permit covers only labor the owner performs. Inspections need 24 hours of notice, and voicemail requests are not accepted.

Warmer months bring property maintenance inspections, and inspectors carry a city-issued photo ID. Ask to see it, and if a notice arrives, clear the violation before listing.

How does a deed transfer through the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office?

Cuyahoga County folded the old auditor, recorder and engineer jobs into one Fiscal Officer. Each deed rides with a DTE 100 statement of value, or a DTE 100 EX if the sale claims an exemption. County standards allow about three business days to review an ordinary instrument, which must carry the parcel number and site address.

  • Recording: the county posts $39 for pages one and two and $8 per extra page, in force since October 24, 2024 (Senate Bill 94).
  • Transfer tax: Ohio Revised Code 322.02 lets a county levy up to thirty cents per hundred dollars on the grantor before recording.
  • Rate: your closing agent can quote Cuyahoga County's conveyance charge for your price.

The division answers at 216-443-2060. Its Great Estates Program helps heirs avoid delay and cost, and a Property Alerts service flags suspicious filings against a parcel.

Which Strongsville sellers are exempt from the Ohio disclosure form?

The state form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 has exemptions. The statute excuses a seller who inherited the house and did not occupy it in the prior year, as well as estate fiduciaries, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, foreclosures and court-ordered sales.

A covered seller owes every buyer a signed copy promptly. A buyer who receives it only after a contract exists may rescind in writing within three business days, and no later than 30 days after acceptance or the closing.

Permit inspections, which need 24 hours of notice, and property maintenance checks in the warmer months. Call 440-580-3105 to ask what applies to your address and whether any permits are still open.

What does it cost to record a deed in Cuyahoga County?

The county's fee is $39 for the first two pages, then $8 for every page after. That schedule began October 24, 2024. Conveyance charges are separate, so request that figure when you book the closing.

Who pays the Cuyahoga County conveyance fee?

The grantor, which means you as the seller. The statute sets the ceiling at thirty cents per hundred dollars, and the county decides what it actually levies.

Can I sell a Strongsville house I inherited?

Yes, after whoever holds legal authority signs the deed. The county's Great Estates Program covers ways to avoid delay in settling an estate.

Do I need a contractor to fix permit problems before selling?

Not always. A homeowner permit exists for work you do yourself at your own residence, but any portion handled by a contractor needs one who has registered with the city.

Where is Grove City and how did it grow?

Grove City lies in southeastern Franklin County, a short drive from downtown Columbus. William F. Breck platted the village east of Broadway in 1852 because the Harrisburg Turnpike already ran toward the capital. The settlers named the place for the groves of trees they left standing when they cleared the land.

The state recognized a village on March 5, 1866, and a city in 1959. The Census Bureau counted 35,575 people in 2010 and 41,252 in 2020, with 45,180 in its 2025 estimate.

A charter written in 1958 and amended in 1982 sets up an elected mayor and council plus an appointed administrator. The city keeps its own police division, which holds national accreditation. Jackson Township staffs four fire stations that cover the city and the township together.

Owners live in roughly seven of every ten Grove City homes, and the median owner-occupied value passes $300,000 in the five-year Census estimates. At that price point most shoppers want a house they can move into, and deferred repairs show up in the offers.

What city rules apply to a Grove City property before a sale?

Sales under a court order, foreclosure sales and sales handled by an estate's fiduciary are carved out. The statute lists every exemption.

How does the deed move through the Franklin County Auditor?

A Grove City deed goes to the Franklin County Auditor's Transfer and Conveyance Department for a stamp and fee before the county recorder files it. The price-based charge is $3 per $1,000, split between $1 from the state and $2 from the county commissioners. A $0.50 transfer tax and a $3 floor sit on top.

  • Figures round up to the next $100 of price.
  • The county share drops away when the seller holds the homestead exemption at transfer, leaving $1 per $1,000.

The Auditor's online calculator returns the amount for a given price. Ask the title company whether it carries the deed to the Auditor for you.

A retail listing works when the house shows well and you can sit through weeks of marketing. Selling alone works for someone who reads contracts comfortably and has watched what nearby homes bring. A direct cash purchase is built for the inherited house, the rental with tenants, or the property with deferred work and a hard moving date.

They can. The Building and Zoning Division cites tall weeds, noxious plants and inoperable vehicles, and a buyer's inspector may notice the same things. Clear them first and call 614-277-3075 if you are unsure what the division has on file.

Usually not. R.C. 5302.30 exempts a transfer by an estate's fiduciary and a seller who inherited the house and did not live there in the prior year. Confirm your situation with a title agent or attorney.

How can a Fairfield, Ohio homeowner sell quickly?

The statute exempts transfers to a buyer who has lived in the home as a personal residence for at least a year, and transfers to a spouse or to a lineal relative, so a sale to a tenant or family member may skip it.

Where is Fairfield and how did it grow?

Fairfield is a city in southern Butler County, about 25 miles north of Cincinnati, on the east bank of the Great Miami River. It formed in 1955 from part of Fairfield Township and absorbed the old hamlets of Symmes Corner, Fair Play, Furmandale and Stockton. Symmes Corner, at Pleasant Avenue and Nilles Road, is now the town center. Fair Play, on the river's east bank, was known for Ohio's first paper mill before a flood in the late 1800s destroyed it. Stockton began as Jones Station on the rail line, and Furmandale, at Winton and Nilles roads, was nicknamed Snaptown. The Miami and Erie Canal ran a few miles east and carried farm goods before the railroad arrived.

The land belonged to the Symmes Purchase of 1788. The Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton Railway, now CSX, came through in the 1850s, and a rail line still bisects the city. Farming dominated until the mid twentieth century, when Hamilton's industry spread south and Fisher Body built a plant at State Route 4 and Symmes Road. The village passed 5,000 residents by 1960 and became a statutory city, and the Interstate 275 beltway in the late 1970s brought commuters from north of Cincinnati.

Most of the city sits above the Great Miami Buried Valley Aquifer, which supplies drinking water to Fairfield, Hamilton and Cincinnati. The city's boundaries reach Hamilton on the north, West Chester on the east and Springdale and Forest Park on the south, and a small part crosses into Hamilton County with no residents. Public transit comes from the Butler County Regional Transit Authority and the Southwest Ohio Regional Transit Authority.

  • The DTE Form 100 or 100EX must be complete, with a valid legal description attached to the deed.
  • Contact the Engineer's Office at 513-867-5744 to have the legal description pre-approved before you submit.

The Recorder's Office holds the recorded deed, and its number is 513-887-3196. The Auditor's records start in 1993, and the Recorder's electronic records reach back to 1987. The Recorder also offers a free fraud alert service called Fraudsleuth that emails you when a document is recorded under your name, which is worth joining before you list. Deeds older than 1987 may require a visit to the Recorder's office to search the paper books, so start early if a title question could delay your closing.

How did Huber Heights get its start?

Huber Heights grew out of Wayne Township, settled in the early to mid 1800s, and became a city on January 23, 1981. It is named for Charles Huber, the developer who built many of the houses that later made up the city. Suburban building began in 1956, and the city later annexed land in Miami County. A small parcel in Greene County was detached in 2013.

The city covers 22.37 square miles as a Dayton suburb. The Census Bureau counted 38,101 residents in 2010 and 43,439 in 2020, a 14% jump that was the largest gain in Montgomery County that decade.

Location drives the local economy. The city sits near the junction of I-70 and I-75, has two I-70 exits lined with chain restaurants, and has long been a base for trucking firms. Freight, logistics and manufacturing names in the city include ABF Freight, Dayton Freight, Coca-Cola and Metokote. What do Huber Heights zoning and building rules require?

The city issues zoning permits for new buildings and accessory structures, exterior alterations, room additions, garages, sheds, carports, pergolas, hot tubs and pools two feet or deeper. Each permit has a $30 application fee and is usually issued within about a week.

The city lists items that need no city permit: fences, driveways, uncovered patios, decks, roof repairs, solar panels and interior work. Many of those do need a permit and inspection from the Montgomery County Building Department, which the city uses as its own building authority. Decks, electrical, heating and air, plumbing, roof repairs and solar panels are on the county's list, and the county can be reached at 937-225-4622.

The Code Enforcement Division posts monthly violation reports, so you can see whether your address has an open case. Resolve any open violation before you list. The permits page lists the forms.

What landlord reporting rule does Huber Heights have?

Chapter 192.21 of the city code requires owners of rental property to file a report with the Tax Administrator within 30 days after a tenant moves in, giving the tenant's name, address and telephone number if known. A second report is due within 30 days after the tenant leaves, with the move-out date and a forwarding address. Owners who miss the reports can be fined up to $100 for each unreported tenant.

If you are selling a rental, file any outstanding reports first, then give the buyer's agent the current tenant details. The city's landlord page carries the form. The permits page also has an application for short-term rental information and the hotel tax form.

  • The statute covers sales, land installment contracts, leases with an option to buy and exchanges of one to four unit homes.
  • A transfer in a divorce settlement, to a government body, or of brand-new, never-occupied construction is exempt.
  • A signed acknowledgment from the buyer completes the exchange.

See the full text of the statute.

What does the Montgomery County Auditor require for a Huber Heights deed?

Montgomery County treats a deed transfer through the Auditor as the step that makes the transfer legal. The county charges a mandatory conveyance and transfer fee of $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price plus $.50 for each parcel. The Auditor's deed transfer line is 937-225-4373, and filings can be made electronically through ePN or Simplifile.

The statement of value that goes with the deed must show the full consideration, including any mortgage the buyer takes on, under R.C. 319.202. Parcels in the Miami County part of Huber Heights go through the Miami County Auditor, so ask that office for its rates and procedure. The county's deed transfer page has the forms.

When does a cash sale fit a Huber Heights seller?

A direct sale suits owners with a deadline, a tenant-occupied house, or a house with repairs they cannot fund. The city can fine an owner up to $100 for each unreported tenant. Reports are due within 30 days after a move-in and again within 30 days after a move-out.

What comes first when I decide to sell in Cleveland Heights?

Cleveland Heights is a inner-ring suburb east of Cleveland, in Cuyahoga County, and it handles resale houses differently from many Ohio towns. How does the Point-of-Sale inspection work?

A city inspector reviews the house and issues a Certificate of Inspection, which the seller must hand to the buyer before the sales contract is executed. The city's page applies this to single-family and two-family homes, duplexes, apartments, condominiums and commercial buildings.

  • Cost: $200 for the first unit and $50 for each additional unit. The city's own examples are $250 for a two-family house and $350 for a four-unit building.

Inspectional Services sets the dollar amount from average repair prices multiplied by 125% for an average-sized Cleveland Heights home. The city's examples are $6,250 for a roof and $5,625 for painting a single-family house. Your real cost may run higher or lower. You may instead submit a signed agreement with a contractor who is registered and bonded with the city, and the city may accept that estimate. A 203K, FNMA or similar rehab loan can stand in for cash if it covers every Class A item. Held funds are released only on written city authorization, and partial releases are possible once substantial progress is shown.

What does the city need before it lets title transfer?

Inspectional Services must receive three items and then send the title company a release letter, and this applies to every sale in the city whether or not escrow is owed. The table sets out the sequence.

Release of a Cleveland Heights property for transfer, per the city's escrow requirements page
StepWhat is submittedWho usually provides it
1Acknowledgement form signed by the buyerBuyer, collected by the seller or agent
2Title company name, escrow officer, address, phone and faxTitle company
3Letter stating the required escrow amount is held, if escrow appliesTitle company
4Release letter sent to the title companyInspectional Services

If the property is not released, the city says a court summons may be issued. Send the first three items early, because the release letter is what lets the closing go forward.

What kind of place is Cleveland Heights for a home seller?

Cleveland Heights sits atop the Portage Escarpment, a ridge that gives the east side a higher elevation than downtown Cleveland. It covers about 8 square miles, with roughly 5,600 residents per square mile in the 2020 count. The first road through the area, Mayfield Road, was built in 1828. The place organized as a hamlet in 1901, became a village in 1903 and a city on August 9, 1921, and grew mostly in the streetcar era.

Many houses date from that early boom, and the Euclid Golf Allotment is on the National Register of Historic Places. The Stadium Square district along Taylor Road is known for Tudor Revival buildings from the 1920s. Coventry Village is the best-known shopping street, and the city has seven parks, among them Cain Park and Forest Hill Park.

The Census Bureau estimates 43,750 residents for July 1, 2025, down 3.5% from the April 2020 base. Owners live in 58.2% of homes, a far higher share than in neighboring Cleveland. The median owner-occupied home value is $192,100 on the 2020-2024 survey, and median gross rent is $1,216. There are 19,323 households, 19.2% of residents are 65 or older, and 58.7% of adults hold a bachelor's degree. A 2020 census tally found 22,270 housing units with 10.0% vacant.

Which schools and transit serve Cleveland Heights?

Most of the city belongs to the Cleveland Heights-University Heights City School District, which has six elementary schools inside city limits, two middle schools and Cleveland Heights High School. A small northwest corner lies in the East Cleveland City School District. Private options include Beaumont School, Lutheran High School East, Horizon Montessori, Ruffing Montessori and the Hebrew Academy of Cleveland.

The Greater Cleveland Regional Transit Authority runs bus service in the city. Because buyers ask about district boundaries, tell your agent or your buyer which district your street falls in.

How does lake-effect snow affect houses in the Heights?

The land rises quickly east of the lake, and the Heights lie where the Snow Belt begins, so seasonal snowfall approaching 100 inches is not unusual there. Lake-effect snow typically runs from mid-November until Lake Erie freezes in late January or early February. Cleveland's 30-year normal precipitation is 41.03 inches a year.

That climate explains why the city's Class A list names roofs, chimneys, downspouts, paint and windows. If you have an older roof or peeling exterior paint, expect the inspector to flag it and plan for either the repair or the escrow.

What are the Cuyahoga County steps after the sale price is agreed?

Cuyahoga County's Fiscal Office handles transfer and recording at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, in Cleveland, with office hours Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and recording hours ending at 4:00 p.m. Every transfer must come with either the DTE 100 statement of value or the DTE 100-EX exemption statement. The standard recording fee rose on October 24, 2024 to $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that, under Senate Bill 94. Call 216-443-2060 with questions.

Property tax is billed separately. Ohio's House Bill 920 of 1976 lowers a district's effective rate as values climb during reappraisals, and the Cuyahoga County Treasurer posts rates by community. Ask the Fiscal Office or your closing agent for the current figure on your parcel.

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 also asks most sellers of homes with one to four units to give the buyer a signed property disclosure form, with exceptions for estates, inheritors who never lived there and transfers between family members in a direct line.

More questions about Cleveland Heights, OH

Can I accept an offer before the Point-of-Sale inspection is done?

No. The city requires the Certificate of Inspection before you enter into an agreement to sell, and the buyer receives a copy before the contract is executed. Book the inspection first, then list or negotiate.

What happens if repairs are not finished by closing?

Major Class A violations still open at transfer require escrowed funds, set at 125% of average repair prices for an average-sized home. A signed contract with a city-registered, bonded contractor, or a rehab loan covering every Class A item, may be accepted in place of cash.

How long does a Cleveland Heights Certificate of Inspection last?

It is valid for one year from the date of issuance. If your house sits unsold for longer than that, a new inspection is needed before you sign a contract.

Which school district serves my Cleveland Heights house?

Most addresses are in the Cleveland Heights-University Heights City School District. A small area on the northwest side belongs to the East Cleveland City School District, so check your street before you describe the schools.

Where is a Cleveland Heights deed recorded?

At the Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland. The deed needs a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX form, and your title company normally files both.

What should a seller know about Reynoldsburg's size and housing?

Reynoldsburg is a Columbus suburb with a large retail base and a mix of owners and renters. Federal estimates for July 2025 show 43,350 people, 5.5% more than the 2020 base of 41,074, living on 11.12 square miles of land in 17,280 households.

Wikipedia says the area was first settled in 1802 and platted in 1831 as Frenchtown, and the present name was fixed in 1893. Local pride centers on the tomato: the city bills itself the Birthplace of the Tomato, and its festival has run each August since 1965. Blacklick Creek runs through town, and Blacklick Woods, a 643-acre Metro Park that opened in 1948 as the first in Franklin County, lies within the city.

Three numbers frame pricing: 61.6% of homes are owner-occupied, the midpoint value is $244,300 and the midpoint rent is $1,259.

Why do three counties touch Reynoldsburg?

The city reaches into Franklin, Fairfield and Licking counties, each with a separate auditor and treasurer. Council legislation from 2026 mentions a Taylor Road annexation in Etna Township and Summit Road work shared with Licking County, so a parcel near that edge may answer to a different office.

City council resolutions for 2026 show how this works in practice: the clerk certifies nuisance costs to both the Franklin County Auditor and the Licking County Auditor for collection, and the city certifies its tax levies to both. If the city ever billed you for cleanup on the lot, ask which county auditor holds the charge before closing.

What does the Reynoldsburg Building Department require?

The Building Division administers four codes, Ohio Building, Residential, Property Maintenance and Flood Damage Prevention, plus the National Electrical Code, and it issues certificates of occupancy and permits for building, electrical, heating, plumbing, sign, sidewalk and flood hazard work. It sits at 7232 East Main Street and answers at 614-322-6802.

  • Residential plan review starts with a permit application, construction drawings and a $100 non-refundable deposit.
  • Plumbing plan review and inspection run through Franklin County Public Health, at 280 East Broad Street in Columbus, not through the city.
  • Contractors register each year with a $75 fee, proof of liability coverage of at least $500,000 and a state license where one applies.
  • Inspections requested by 3 p.m. through the automated line, 614-322-6821, are generally done the next business day, though the city has up to four days.

Inspectors working for buyers tend to ask about permits for decks, basement finishes and plumbing changes, so gather those records early.

Does Reynoldsburg regulate short-term rentals?

The city's 2026 legislation page lists an ordinance to establish Section 705, Permitting Short-Term Rentals, as a chapter of the codified ordinances. An owner who rents a house by the night, and wants to sell it to another host, should ask the city whether any permit passes to a new owner.

The same list shows a council action in 2026 to expand the Eastern Community Reinvestment Area, which allows property tax abatement, and several agreements for tax exemption on new projects. Ask the city whether your address sits inside an abatement district before you tell a buyer an abatement is available.

Who works and shops in Reynoldsburg, and does it help a sale?

Yes, since local jobs feed buyer demand. Wikipedia draws on the city's 2021 audit, which names Victoria's Secret and Bath & Body Works companies, Reynoldsburg City Schools, Kroger, Walmart and the State of Ohio among the biggest employers. The Ohio Department of Agriculture, the Ohio Fire Academy and the Office of the State Fire Marshal are also based in the city.

QuickFacts reports 2022 retail sales of about $1.69 billion, or $41,071 per resident, which is far above the other three cities in its comparison. The median household earns $72,972, commutes average 25.2 minutes, and 68.7% of residents aged 16 and up are in the labor force. A listing can point to nearby shopping and a manageable drive without naming a subdivision.

How do Reynoldsburg schools and parks shape listings?

The majority of the city is in Reynoldsburg City Schools, which Wikipedia says runs seven elementary schools, two junior highs and a high school with two campuses, Livingston and Summit. The city's parks department manages 275 acres of parkland across nine major parks, in addition to Blacklick Woods.

Buyers searching online often filter by school, so name the buildings that serve your street, such as Herbert Mills, Rosehill or Slate Ridge Elementary, only after you have confirmed the attendance zone with the district.

What checklist helps before you list a Reynoldsburg house?

A short list of calls and records can shorten the sale, whichever route you choose.

  • Confirm the county on your tax bill and the date of the next installment.
  • Pull permits for every deck, basement, furnace or plumbing change, and ask Franklin County Public Health about any plumbing approval.
  • Ask the Building Department about open code violation notices or citations on the address.
  • Check for a nuisance charge that the city sent to the county auditor.
  • Write down which Reynoldsburg elementary and junior high serve the street.

These answers also help a direct buyer make a firmer offer, because fewer unknowns remain at the closing table.

What should you know about Franklin County tax bills on a Reynoldsburg sale?

Franklin County set collection dates of March 2, 2026 and July 20, 2026 for the 2025 tax year, and payments after July 20 carry penalty and interest, the Treasurer says. Values are reset on a six-year cycle with a midpoint update, and between cycles they move only for physical changes, demolition or a Board of Revision ruling.

An owner disputing the 2026 value can file with the Auditor from November 20, 2026 until March 31, 2027. Qualifying owners who are 65, disabled or certain surviving spouses may use the Homestead credit, and the Auditor says its decision follows verification that total income does not exceed $41,000. The Treasurer's office, 614-525-3438, gives the amount owed on a given parcel.

Reynoldsburg fees and Franklin County dates for sellers

Which Reynoldsburg sellers choose a cash sale?

Owners with deferred repairs, an unclosed permit or a departing tenant often pick it, because they value a set closing date over a long listing period. A buyer with a loan brings an appraisal and an inspection, and either can delay a sale or prompt repair requests.

Direct buyers typically take the house as-is. Get each offer in writing, learn who pays closing costs and read the settlement statement before signing day.

More questions about Reynoldsburg, OH

Which counties is Reynoldsburg in?

Reynoldsburg lies in Franklin, Fairfield and Licking counties, according to Wikipedia. Check your parcel to see which county auditor and treasurer bill your property.

Who handles plumbing permits in Reynoldsburg?

Franklin County Public Health reviews plumbing plans and schedules plumbing inspections for the city, per the city's Building Department page. Once a plan is approved, the permit application goes to the city's Building Division.

Does Reynoldsburg permit short-term rentals?

The city's 2026 legislation list includes an ordinance establishing Section 705, Permitting Short-Term Rentals. Ask the city for the current permit rules before listing a house that is used as a rental.

When was the second half of the 2025 Franklin County tax bill due?

July 20, 2026. After that date the Treasurer adds penalty and interest, and not receiving a bill does not change that.

How big are Reynoldsburg households?

The 2020 to 2024 count is 17,280 households with 2.38 people each on average. Roughly 61.6% are owned by the people living in them.

Lancaster at a glance

Selling in Lancaster?

How fast can a Lancaster house sell, and which route is best?

The route you choose sets the pace in Lancaster. An agent listing takes the longest because of showings and a buyer's loan, a by-owner sale moves at the pace you can manage, and a cash buyer can close once title work is clear.

  • Agent sale: right for a house that shows well and an owner with patience.
  • Owner sale: trims the fee and adds tasks, from the disclosure form to the deed packet.
  • Cash sale: made for inherited houses, rentals and homes whose repair list outruns the budget.

Lancaster is a growing city. Federal estimates show 41,956 people living here in mid 2025, 3.5 percent more than the 40,543 counted in April 2020, and 59.1 percent of households own their home. That growth is a point in favor of selling here.

What is Lancaster's history, and what did glass have to do with it?

Lancaster was founded in 1800 where Zane's Trace crossed the Hocking River, three years before Ohio became a state. It was first called New Lancaster, took its shorter name by an act of the legislature in 1805, and was incorporated in 1831. The Lancaster Lateral Canal opened in 1834 and linked local farms to eastern markets. German settlers, many from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, shaped the early town.

Glass made the city's name. The nickname is Glass City, the Ohio Glass Museum downtown records more than a century of the industry, and Anchor Hocking ranks second on the city's 2021 employer list. Two Lancaster natives are remembered at the Sherman House, built in 1811: General William Tecumseh Sherman and his brother, Senator John Sherman. The Georgian Museum, built in 1832, stands in one of Lancaster's three national historic districts.

Older houses near downtown sit beside newer subdivisions on the edges, across a city of roughly 18.85 square miles. The Fairfield County Fair, always the last county fair of the Ohio season, fills the second week of October.

Which employers and commuting patterns shape Lancaster's market?

Health care, glass and government anchor the local job market. Wikipedia reproduces the list from the city's 2021 financial report, shown here.

RankEmployerEmployees
1Fairfield Medical Center2,314

3Fairfield County1,387

5Kroger936

Some residents work at the hospital, county offices and plants, and others drive toward Columbus, about 33 miles northwest. Workers here average 27.7 minutes to reach their jobs, the longest commute among Kent, Kettering, Lakewood and Lancaster. The median household earns $59,133, and a typical owned home is worth $193,900, the lowest figure of those four cities. Households average 2.38 people, children under 18 make up 22.7 percent of the population, and 21.9 percent of adults have a bachelor's degree, which fits a family oriented town with modest prices.

What should a Lancaster seller know about schools, weather and the house itself?

Lancaster City Schools serve the city, with Lancaster High School as the public high school, and Ohio University Lancaster operates a branch campus. The public library is a branch of the Fairfield County District Library. The River Valley Mall and downtown make up the main shopping areas, and the Fairfield County Airport sits about 3.5 miles northwest of the central business district. The Lancaster Eagle-Gazette, Ohio's longest continuously operating newspaper, still covers the city, which makes it a handy place to check local news that touches property values.

  • Moisture: NOAA normals credited on Wikipedia give Lancaster about 40 inches of yearly rain and snowmelt, falling on roughly 118 days.
  • Winter: January lows average 21.5 degrees and the coldest reading on record is minus 12, so heating systems and exposed pipes get a real test.
  • Summer: July highs average 85 degrees, with a record of 100 degrees, which makes cooling and attic ventilation fair questions for buyers.

Keep receipts for roof, furnace and water heater work, and hand them to the buyer with the disclosure form.

How do Lancaster's nightly rental rules affect a sale?

Yes, when the house being sold is rented by the night. Lancaster's zoning code includes a Short Term Rentals chapter, 1131, which council took up in a 2025 ordinance after the City Planning Commission voted on June 26, 2025 to recommend it. Check the current text with the city's Community Development Department.

  • Definition: a dwelling with up to five guestrooms, rented for stays under 30 days in a row.
  • Permit: a zoning clearance permit is required for each short term rental, renewed every two years, with a renewal deadline of the first Monday in November of the year the permit expires.
  • Local host: the host must be able to respond to an emergency within one hour.
  • Occupancy permit: the Building Department issues one before the first rental.

The chapter says a change in ownership voids the current permit and calls for a new application. Any buyer who wants to keep renting the house by the night will have to apply again, so say so at the first showing.

How does the Fairfield County Auditor process a Lancaster deed?

As the Fairfield County seat, Lancaster has the County Auditor's office right in town, at 108 N. High Street, and the doors close to filers at four in the afternoon. The Auditor's fact sheet lists a transfer fee of $.50 per parcel and a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes hands.

  • Legal description first: the prepared deed goes to the Auditor's Map Room, by email at maproom@fairfieldcountyohio.gov, for approval before the transfer desk accepts it.
  • Documents: a deed and a DTE 100 conveyance fee statement, or a DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers.
  • Delivery: in person, by mail to Attn: Conveyance, or electronically through Simplifile.
  • Recording: afterward, the Fairfield County Recorder, at (740) 652-7100, records the deed.

Ohio Revised Code 319.202 puts the fee on the seller and requires the buyer to submit the value statement. Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 calls for the disclosure form on residential property of up to four units, and its exceptions cover estate fiduciary transfers and inherited property the seller has not lived in for a year.

Should a Lancaster seller choose a cash buyer?

Cash earns a look when a conventional sale would stall over repairs, a cloudy title or a tight deadline. In Lancaster that often describes a house with old mechanical systems, a rental with tenants, or an estate with several heirs.

Get a written offer that names the closing date and says who pays title and recording costs. Compare the Auditor's fee against the closing statement, and keep the signed disclosure form in your own file. Offers from two or three buyers, plus an agent's estimate of net proceeds, will show whether the speed is worth the discount.

More questions about Lancaster, OH

How much is the Fairfield County conveyance fee on a Lancaster house?

The County Auditor's fact sheet lists $4.00 per thousand of consideration plus a $.50 per parcel transfer fee. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 makes the grantor responsible.

Where does a Lancaster deed get dropped off?

The Fairfield County Auditor's transfer desk at 108 N. High Street takes it once the Map Room approves the legal description. Standard weekday hours run until 4:00 p.m.

Can I sell my Lancaster home as is?

Yes, but you still complete the Ohio disclosure form that Revised Code 5302.30 requires for homes of up to four units. A financed buyer may ask for repairs after an inspection, while a cash buyer builds them into the price.

Does a nightly rental permit carry over to a Lancaster buyer?

No. The city's short term rental chapter says a change in ownership voids the current zoning clearance permit and requires a new application. Confirm the current rules with the city's Community Development Department.

What is the typical commute from Lancaster?

Workers in Lancaster average 27.7 minutes to get to their jobs, according to Census Bureau figures. Columbus sits about 33 miles northwest of the city.
