How does Findlay's housing market work for a seller?

Findlay is the seat of Hancock County and the second-largest city in Northwest Ohio, roughly 40 miles south of Toledo. Many of its buyers work for the big employers covered below, including Marathon Petroleum, Whirlpool and the regional hospital.

The Blanchard River cuts across town from east to west. The settlement began as Fort Findlay, a stockade raised in the War of 1812, and the first lots were platted in 1821. Oil and gas drilling in the 1880s lifted the population from 4,633 in 1880 to 18,553 by 1890. Subdivisions fill the rest of the 19.64 square miles of land.

An owner in town can hire an agent, go it alone, or deal with an investor directly, and the local details below change the math for each.

How pricey is a Findlay home by the Census numbers?

Findlay's median owned-home value of $191,000 sits below the $332,700 shown for the United States in the same Census tables. About 40 percent of households rent, so landlords and first-time buyers both shop here.

The 2020 count was 40,313, close to the 2025 estimate, so rival listings rather than newcomers cap what a house fetches.

Other Census figures help frame a buyer: 91.0 percent of households have a broadband subscription, 30.6 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and the city counts 2,139 veterans. Remote workers weighing a Findlay purchase will read the broadband line first.

How does the Blanchard River affect selling a Findlay house?

Flood exposure is the first property-specific question Findlay buyers and lenders raise. The river crested at 18.46 feet in 2007, causing around $100 million in damage and coming close to the 1913 record.

The city floodplain page lays out what an owner should know:

  • The city participates in the National Flood Insurance Program, so any parcel can be insured through it or a private carrier.
  • Grading, new construction and alterations inside a Special Flood Hazard Area need a Flood Development Permit before work begins.
  • Structural damage in that area, from flood, fire, wind or anything else, goes to the Zoning Department for a damage assessment.
  • The Hancock County Auditor maps show whether a given parcel sits in the hazard area, and zoning staff will help read them.

After the first phase of river benching, the city sent FEMA a Letter of Map Revision proposing to remove or shrink flood zones over a significant amount of land, and the flood information page links a parcel list. See whether your lot is named before choosing a list price, since a revised map can lower or raise a buyer's insurance premium.

Weather also tests the structure. NOAA normals on the city's Wikipedia page show about 37.7 inches of precipitation and 23.8 inches of snow a year, so buyers poke at roof edges, downspouts and damp basement corners.

Which Findlay employers and roads feed buyer demand?

Marathon Petroleum has its headquarters downtown, Whirlpool operates what is considered the world's largest dishwasher plant by output, and Lowe's, Kohl's, Best Buy and Campbell Soup run distribution centers here. Cooper Tire, founded in Findlay in 1914, came under Goodyear in 2021.

The largest local payrolls, per the 2024 city financial report quoted on Wikipedia:

  • Blanchard Valley Regional Health Center, 3,165 employees
  • Marathon Petroleum, 2,159
  • Whirlpool, 1,930
  • Goodyear, 895
  • Findlay City Schools, 865
  • The University of Findlay, 548

Interstate 75 crosses the city, US 68 ends here, and US 224 plus Ohio routes 12, 15, 37 and 568 all pass through. The University of Findlay enrolls over 4,100 students and Owens Community College adds more,. Public school students attend Findlay City Schools, and Findlay High School covers grades 9 to 12.

What does Hancock County charge to transfer a Findlay deed?

The county Auditor takes $3 for every thousand dollars conveyed, rounded to the nearest ten cents, and adds $0.50 per parcel. Some transfers are exempt from the conveyance portion.

According to the Hancock County property transfer page, the Auditor needs a DTE 100 statement of value (or a DTE 100(EX) when an exemption applies) and a notarized deed whose legal description is exact. Checks are written to the Hancock County Auditor. Staff in the Real Estate Division, room 21 of the courthouse, take questions at 419-424-7015.

Filing with the recorder comes next. The recorder's fee schedule charges $39 for the first two pages of a document and $8 for each additional page, a rate that began in January 2025. Ohio requires the signature on the deed to be acknowledged before a notary or similar officer (ORC 5301.01).

What else shapes a Findlay neighborhood besides the river?

Findlay brands itself Flag City, USA, and the calendar gives buyers a feel for daily life: Boogie on the Block in June, the Flag City BalloonFest in August, then Oktoberfest and a Halloween parade in the fall, with the Hancock County Fair as an anchor.

The Findlay Reservoir No. 2, at roughly 5 billion gallons, is the largest above-ground reservoir in Ohio. Riverside Park holds the weir on the Blanchard, the Findlay-Hancock County Public Library has served the city since 1888, and the University of Findlay runs a 152-acre farm for its equestrian and pre-veterinary students. Findlay Airport lies about two nautical miles south-southwest of the central business district. Touch-tone telephone service debuted in Findlay on November 1, 1960, and for about three months the city was the only place in the world that had it.

Mention them in a listing: a short drive to the park, school or plant gate is often the first question.

What must a Findlay seller hand the buyer?

Ohio's residential disclosure statute (ORC 5302.30) has the seller fill in a condition form for the buyer. Late delivery opens a three business day window for the buyer to walk away.

The statute exempts estate fiduciaries, heirs who never lived in the home and family transfers, a list that fits Findlay's many long-held family houses.

What are the practical ways to sell a Findlay house?

Your repair list and your deadline decide which route fits.

  • Agent listing: the most exposure, with closing set by showings and the buyer's lender.
  • Sale by owner: no commission, but forms and deed prep are yours.
  • Cash purchase: no lender or appraisal, and you pick the closing day, at a price that reflects the repairs.
  • Family or neighbor sale: friendlier talks and the same Auditor paperwork.

Line up two written offers and compare what each leaves you after fees, tax proration and payoff.

More questions about Findlay, OH

Does a Findlay home near the river sell for less?

It can, since flood insurance adds a cost for the buyer. Pull the parcel on the Hancock County Auditor maps, ask Zoning about the pending map revision, and keep any elevation certificate or insurance records handy.

What is the Hancock County conveyance fee?

The Auditor charges $3 per $1,000 conveyed and $0.50 per parcel, with recording billed separately by the recorder. Call the Real Estate Division for the total on your deed.

Do I have to repair a Findlay house before selling?

Ohio sets no repair requirement for a sale. Known problems go on the disclosure form, and a lender-backed buyer may negotiate fixes after the inspection.

Where is the deed filed once a Findlay sale closes?

With the Hancock County Recorder, once the Auditor has endorsed it. Until recorded, a deed is fraudulent against a later good-faith buyer (ORC 5301.25), so closers file fast.

Who buys houses in Findlay besides families?

How do Hilliard homeowners usually sell, and what sets this city apart?

Owners in Hilliard can hire an agent, market the house themselves, or accept a purchase from a company that pays cash and takes the property in its current state. The city's strong school district, high incomes and mix of 1950s subdivisions, Old Hilliard blocks and newer neighborhoods make it a place where condition and presentation drive the price.

Sellers here deal with Hilliard's planning staff on zoning and exterior rules, with the Franklin County Auditor on the deed, and with Ohio's disclosure statute. The sections below walk through each, along with the Census figures that describe who is buying.

What is Hilliard's history and where does it sit in Franklin County?

Hilliard sits in western Franklin County between Big Darby Creek and the Scioto River, bordered by Columbus, Upper Arlington, Dublin and Galloway. John Reed Hilliard bought about 10 acres of farmland in 1852 and platted the town on September 1, 1853 around a Piqua and Indiana Railroad station, so the place started as Hilliard's Station.

The village incorporated on July 13, 1869 with 280 residents. Three large subdivisions in the 1950s set off rapid growth, and Hilliard reached city status on December 12, 1960 with 5,633 people. Hookups to the regional water and sewer systems in the 1960s and the finished I-270 Outerbelt in the early 1970s drove a second wave.

The historic district along Norwich Street preserves older houses, and the restored original train station stands in Weaver Park. Cemetery Road and Main Street (Hilliard Rome Road) carry most local traffic, and I-270 reaches the city's eastern edge, with a park and ride on Cemetery Road close to the interchange.

Community landmarks include the Early Television Museum, the Franklin County Fair, the Old Hilliardfest art and street fair, a Fourth of July parade and the summer Celebration at the Station concerts. Buyers who tour the city often see those events, so a house within reach of Old Hilliard or a park carries that appeal into its listing.

What do the latest Census numbers say about Hilliard housing?

Hilliard has the highest median household income and home value of the four Ohio cities in the Census comparison used for these pages. A buyer pool with that profile expects clean, updated houses and will compare yours with newer construction in the same school zone.

Which schools and services cover a Hilliard address?

The Hilliard City School District covers the city, the old Brown and Norwich township areas, part of Columbus, and sections of Dublin and Galloway. It runs fourteen elementary schools, two sixth-grade schools (Station and Tharp), three middle schools (Heritage, Weaver and Memorial) and three high schools: Darby, Davidson and Bradley.

Saint Brendan School (K-8, Roman Catholic) and Sunrise Academy (K-8, Islamic) are in the city too. Because the district reaches past the city line, ask the district which school your exact address feeds.

  • Norwich Township Fire Department provides fire and medical response for the city.
  • The recreation department manages more than 25 parks, and the Heritage Rail Trail starts on Center Street in Old Hilliard.
  • Voters approved a 0.5% income tax increase in November 2021 to pay for a recreation and wellness campus, backed by bonds of up to $95 million.

Which Hilliard planning rules should a seller check?

The Planning Division enforces Hilliard's zoning and property maintenance code and handles zoning certificates, property inspections, sign and fence permits, and zoning violation reports. Applications and fees go through the city's OpenGov portal.

The city warns that scammers email residents posing as city staff and demand payment for permits. Fees are paid only through the portal on an application you started, and the city does not send surprise invoices.

If you have rented the house, read the short-term rental rules first. City council amended chapters 1105, 1115, 1121 and 1141 on July 11, 2022 after finding that short-term rentals were not a permitted use, and the change tested the use in Old Hilliard with a review planned one year later. Ask the Planning Division what applies to your parcel today. The Planning Division page has contact details.

What does Ohio require a Hilliard seller to disclose?

Most Hilliard home sales trigger the state's residential disclosure form under R.C. 5302.30. You fill it in, sign and date it, and hand it to the buyer early, and the buyer countersigns to show receipt.

  • The form asks about the water supply, the sewer, the structure and any hazardous materials, plus defects you personally know of.
  • It carries no warranty, and the statute pushes buyers toward their own inspection.
  • You answer only for what you actually knew, so an honest mistake does not create liability.

Gifts to a spouse or lineal relatives, splits between co-owners, government transfers and sales to a buyer who already lived in the house for a year skip the form. The statute text has the complete list.

What happens at the Franklin County Auditor when a Hilliard house sells?

The Franklin County Auditor will not endorse a Hilliard deed until a value statement is on file under R.C. 319.202. The buyer's side prepares it, and the seller pays the conveyance fee plus any county transfer tax. "Value" means everything paid for the property, including a mortgage the buyer assumes, and willfully misstating it is prohibited.

  • The statement asks about a property tax reduction under R.C. 323.152 and about agricultural use valuation, so tell your buyer if either applied.
  • The office takes cash, business checks and cashier's checks made to the Auditor. It refuses personal checks.
  • A payment that is off by even a little will hold the transfer up.

Use the county's online calculator to see the rate. A closing agent normally carries the deed in.

Who benefits from a quick cash sale in Hilliard?

Owners who cannot fund repairs before listing, who face a fixed deadline, or who inherited a house they do not plan to keep are the usual fit. A conventional listing suits a well-kept house in a school zone buyers want, though shoppers often request an inspection. In either case, add up what you would net after repairs, taxes and monthly carrying costs, and read who pays what at closing.

More questions about Hilliard, OH

Can I rent my Hilliard house on a short-term basis?

Check with the Planning Division first. Hilliard's council reported in 2022 that short-term rentals were not a permitted use, then changed the zoning code on July 11 of that year to try them in Old Hilliard. Your parcel's zoning decides the answer.

Where do I apply for a fence or sign permit in Hilliard?

Use the OpenGov portal run by the Planning Division. Fees are paid there, and the city says it never emails invoices for applications you did not start.

Who fights fires at a Hilliard address?

Norwich Township Fire Department, which serves both the city and the township. Hilliard's police division patrols the township as well.

What paperwork reaches the county auditor on a Hilliard sale?

A statement of value under R.C. 319.202, the deed, and the exact fee. The Auditor endorses the deed once those are in order, and the county recorder then files it.

Does a buyer who rented my house first still get a disclosure form?

Not necessarily. A buyer who lived in the house as a residence for the year before the transfer is exempt under R.C. 5302.30, and so are transfers to close relatives and between co-owners.

What makes selling a house in Warren, Ohio different?

Warren is the seat of Trumbull County, on the Mahoning River about 14 miles northwest of Youngstown and 56 miles southeast of Cleveland. Selling here means working with a city whose rules for rentals, vacant houses and contractors are written into its Codified Ordinances.

For mid-2025 the Census Bureau estimates 38,328 people, below the 39,201 counted in 2020 and the 41,557 counted in 2010. The sections below take the local and county steps in turn, starting with the numbers.

How did Warren's industrial past shape its housing?

The town was founded in 1798 on land bought from the Connecticut Land Company and became the Trumbull County seat in 1801. By 1888 four railroads served it. Packard Electric and Packard Motor Car were both founded in Warren in the 1890s, and steel became a major industry across the county through the 20th century. The Trumbull Steel mill, later part of Republic Steel, kept running under various owners until 2012.

Population followed the mills. Warren peaked at 63,494 in 1970 and has fallen in every census since, to 46,832 in 2000 and 39,201 in 2020. Many late 19th and early 20th century buildings still stand around Courthouse Square. The larger employers now include St. Joseph Warren Hospital, the Tribune Chronicle and Thomas Steel Strip, and Kimberly-Clark announced plans in 2024 for a new paper production facility in the city.

What does it cost to own a home in Warren?

The Census survey covering 2020 through 2024 describes a city of low values and many renters.

  • Owners occupy 56.1% of housing units.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $86,400.
  • Owners pay $967 a month with a mortgage and $409 without one.
  • Gross rent at the midpoint is $766.
  • There are 16,871 households with 2.16 people each.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $37,887, and 31.9% of residents live in poverty.

At these values a repair bill can equal a large part of the price, so buyers weigh condition closely and expect the seller to say what is wrong.

Does a rental in Warren need a dwelling permit?

Yes. Under section 1367.10 of Warren's Codified Ordinances, no dwelling unit that lacks at least one owner living in it can be occupied without a residential non-owner occupied dwelling permit from the Health Officer's office. The permit is issued after a Building Inspector confirms compliance with the Housing, Building, Zoning and fire codes.

  • The annual fee for a single-unit dwelling is $120, and multi-unit buildings pay $100 per unit for two to fifty units, with lower per-unit rates above that.
  • A permit lasts one year and cannot be transferred to a new owner, so whoever buys a tenant-occupied house applies in their own name.
  • The Water Department will not open service for a non-owner-occupied unit without proof of the permit.
  • Occupying a unit without a permit carries a $1,000 fine, and each day counts as a separate violation.

Before listing a rental, ask the Health Department whether the permit is current, and tell the buyer it does not travel with the deed.

When does an empty Warren house count as vacant?

Chapter 1338 sets up a Vacant Property Registry. An owner has 30 days after a structure becomes vacant to register it with the Code Official. The annual fee is $200 for a residential structure, though it can be avoided if the property is secured, free of trash, mowed, and shows a visible address. Missing the filing deadline costs $50 per day up to $1,000.

One rule bears directly on a sale. A house under a signed broker listing agreement is not counted as vacant during the first six months of that listing, while an empty house offered for sale by its owner counts as vacant immediately. If you have moved out and plan to sell without a broker, register or secure the property first.

Vacant structure registrationCode OfficialChapter 1338: register within 30 days of vacancy

Do you need a contractor to fix up a Warren house before selling?

Not always. Chapter 1305 makes contractors register with the city, posting a $25,000 surety bond and showing insurance, yet it exempts a homeowner working on the single-family house they live in. That owner files a waiver of liability with the Building Division, and permits under Chapter 1307 still apply.

A hired contractor must hold the registration first, and one who starts without it pays double the fee. Ask any contractor for the city registration before work begins.

How does the Trumbull County Board of Revision work?

Three county offices, the Auditor, the Treasurer and the Commissioners, or their representatives, make up the board. It rules on value complaints and on denied homestead or owner-occupancy claims, and it leaves the tax dollars on your bill alone. Whoever files carries the burden of proof.

  • Complaints go to the Auditor's office, which acts as the board's secretary. Email goes to BOR@co.trumbull.oh.us. A handwritten form needs a notary, and a typed form sent by email does not.
  • Appraisals, photos, repair estimates and a recent settlement statement and purchase agreement are the evidence types the county names.
  • Notice of a hearing arrives at least ten days ahead, and you may attend in person, by phone or on video.

The filing window under Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 closes at the end of March following the tax year. An outside party can seek a higher value only when a recent arm's length sale beat the listed value by ten percent and by a state threshold, which the county page sets at $567,000 for tax year 2025.

How do Warren's schools and downtown shape buyer interest?

The Warren City School District runs four preK to 8 schools and Warren G. Harding High School. A second high school, Western Reserve, operated on the south side from 1966 to 1990. Declining population led to a redistricting plan, a new Harding building and the demolition of several early 20th century elementary and junior high schools, so a buyer comparing school buildings should ask the district which one serves a given street. The John F. Kennedy Catholic School offers kindergarten through grade 12 on two campuses.

Downtown still centers on the Trumbull County Courthouse, built beginning in 1895, along with a Carnegie Law Library and bank and office buildings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Tribune Chronicle, the daily paper, traces its roots to 1812 in what was the Connecticut Western Reserve.

What does Ohio require when you sell an inherited house?

Many Warren sales start with an estate. Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, an heir who has not lived in the house during the past year is excused from the state disclosure form, and so is a fiduciary selling for an estate, guardianship or trust. Other sellers of one-to-four unit homes must hand over the signed form.

Even then, buyers ask about known defects, so answer in writing and keep a copy.

How do Warren's roads and winters affect showing a house?

A freeway carrying Ohio 82 bypasses the city, and Ohio 5 leads southwest to the Ohio Turnpike. US 422 and Ohio 45 also run through Warren. NOAA normals reproduced for the city list 40.81 inches of precipitation and 27.9 inches of snow per year, with 21 snowy days and a January mean minimum of 16.8 degrees. Plan showings around plowed walks, working heat and visible roof and gutter condition, since buyers check these first in winter.

More questions about Warren, OH

Do I need a permit to sell a rental house in Warren?

The dwelling permit in section 1367.10 does not transfer when the house sells. The buyer applies for a new one, and the Water Department wants proof of it before opening service.

What if I move out and list the house myself?

An empty house offered for sale by its owner counts as vacant under Chapter 1338 and must be registered within 30 days. A broker-listed house gets a six-month pass from the start of the listing.

When is the deadline to dispute my property value in Trumbull County?

By the end of March after the tax year, or the first-half collection date when that is later. The window for tax year 2025 closed March 31, 2026. Call the Auditor at 330-675-2420.

Does an inherited house need the Ohio disclosure form?

Usually not. Section 5302.30 excuses an heir who has not lived in the house for a year and also excuses fiduciaries acting for an estate.

Can I keep my homestead exemption after I sell?

No. The exemption belongs to the home you own and live in on January 1, so it ends with the sale. Your next home needs its own application with the county auditor.

What should you know before selling a house in Westerville, Ohio?

Westerville is a northeast suburb of Columbus that straddles two counties, Franklin and Delaware, and that split decides which auditor, which board of revision and which health district you deal with. The Census Bureau lists 12.60 square miles of land and estimates 38,165 residents on July 1, 2025, down from 39,190 in the 2020 census.

Westerville runs its own electric and water utilities and does not collect property tax at all. The sections below start with where your parcel sits and then walk through the city steps, county filings and state paperwork for a sale.

How did Westerville become the Dry Capital of the World?

Settlers arrived around 1810, and the town took its name from the Westervelt family, who moved from New York in 1818. Otterbein University traces to a seminary chartered in 1839 and was renamed in 1847. The town was platted by 1856 and incorporated in August 1858.

An 1859 ordinance banned alcohol sales, and in 1909 the Anti-Saloon League moved its national headquarters to Westerville. The town stayed dry for most of the 20th century and was known as the Dry Capital of the World. In 1916 Westerville became the first village in Ohio to adopt a council-manager form of government, and the city still runs under it. A 1995 annexation of 941 acres to the north brought in alcohol-selling businesses, and voters later approved alcohol sales at specific locations in the old town.

The old town sits around Uptown Westerville and Otterbein, and the 1995 annexation added land to the north.

What do the Census numbers say about owning in Westerville?

Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 describe a mid-priced suburb with a settled owner base.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 72.5%.

  • Households: 15,208, at 2.43 people per household.
  • Median household income: $109,404; 57.9% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
  • Residents 65 and older: 21.5%.

Mean travel time to work is 19.4 minutes. Interstates 71 and 270 border the city, State Route 3 runs through Uptown as State Street, and central Westerville is about 16 miles from downtown Columbus and 12 miles from John Glenn Columbus International Airport by interstate.

Which county handles your Westerville house?

The city sits across the Franklin and Delaware county line, so start with the auditor's parcel search to see which county bills your house. The city itself collects no property tax. Franklin County Auditor's office is at 614-525-4663 and Delaware County Auditor's office is at 740-833-2900.

Delaware's board says it reviews value as of the January 1 lien date and does not hear complaints about taxes. Hearings usually take 10 to 20 minutes, and an appeal goes to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the decision letter.

What does the Westerville Building Division require?

The Building Division is a state-certified department inside Planning and Development, reachable at 614-901-6650. It reviews plans before work starts and issues a Certificate of Occupancy or a Final Approval after inspections. Permit fees are paid when you pick up the permit, and plans go in through the city's Plan Review Portal.

  • Permits cover new buildings, alterations, signs, fences, pools, patio covers, decks, garages and satellite dishes, and fences carry no permit fee.
  • The city does not require a homeowner or contractor to hold a city license before pulling a permit.
  • A home occupation can need a conditional use permit.
  • Since 2021 the division reports nearly 700 residential permits with about $40.7 million in construction value.

Ask the division for your permit history before you list, and close out any permit that never received a final approval.

How do utilities and trash work when a Westerville house changes hands?

Westerville supplies electric and water service itself, while sewer treatment comes through Columbus and refuse through Rumpke. All four charges appear on one bill that is due on the 15th of the month after it is issued. Utility Billing sits at 21 S. State Street and answers at 614-901-6430. Sewer charges follow water use.

  • Refuse and recycling go out every Tuesday, and yard waste goes out every Monday.
  • Large items such as stoves and furniture can go to the curb on collection day, but air conditioners and refrigerators must go through outside vendors.
  • The city requires owners to keep yards and vacant lots free of trash, debris, overgrown grass and weeds. Code Enforcement takes calls at 614-901-6650.
  • A garage sale needs no permit, but it is limited to one every six months and three consecutive days.

Schedule the final meter reading with Utility Billing as part of the closing checklist so the buyer's service starts clean.

What do snow and storm rules mean for a Westerville seller?

Winter showings run into city rules. Plows clear all city streets once snow passes two inches, and a snow emergency starts automatically above three inches, after which cars left on the street can be towed. Owners must keep the walkway in front of the house clear of snow and ice.

Storms bring a second set of rules. The city removes fallen limbs from street trees, but a tree or branch that comes down from private property is the owner's job to remove. Westerville also offers free residential fire inspections at 614-901-6600, which gives a seller a quick safety check before a buyer's inspector arrives.

Which schools and employers draw buyers to Westerville?

The Westerville City School District has three high schools: South, which is an International Baccalaureate school, North and Central. Its middle schools are Blendon, Genoa, Heritage, Minerva Park and Walnut Springs.

The city's 2023 financial report lists JPMorgan Chase as the top employer at 3,471 workers, followed by Mount Carmel Health System at 3,293, Westerville City Schools at 1,836 and Otterbein University at 1,533. The Central Ohio Transit Authority runs five bus lines through the city, though Westerville operates no buses of its own.

What must an Ohio seller deliver in Westerville?

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 applies to sales of homes with one to four units. The seller completes the state disclosure form and delivers a signed copy to the buyer or the buyer's agent. Receiving it late opens a short rescission window, so hand it over before the offer is signed.

Value disputes follow ORC 5715.19: the complaint is due by March 31 of the next year, or the first-half collection closing date if that falls later. The tax year 2025 window closed March 31, 2026 in both counties.

Does the City of Westerville collect property taxes?

No. The city's service page says county governments collect property taxes for every taxing district. Call the Franklin County Auditor at 614-525-4663 or the Delaware County Auditor at 740-833-2900, depending on where your parcel sits.

Do I need a permit to build a fence before I sell a Westerville house?

Yes, a permit is required to build, replace, relocate or alter a fence, though the city charges no permit fee. Call the Zoning Division at 614-901-6662.

Who collects trash at a Westerville house?

Refuse and recycling are collected Tuesdays and yard waste Mondays, and Rumpke provides refuse service. Containers go out no earlier than 6 p.m. the evening before and no later than 7 a.m. on collection day.

What is Westerville's income tax rate?

The city's service page lists 2.00%, and all adult residents and businesses file city returns. Ask the city's tax office at 614-901-6420 how a sale affects your filing.

How do I find out which county my Westerville house is in?

Search the parcel on either county auditor's website, or look at the property tax bill. Franklin and Delaware counties run separate boards of revision, health districts and auditor offices.

The 2020 census also tallied 14,716 housing units, 3.9% of them empty, with only 1.1% of owned homes vacant.

Which schools, roads and local draws affect a North Ridgeville sale?

Buyers with children look first at the North Ridgeville City School District, which runs an Early Childhood Learning Community, Liberty Elementary, the North Ridgeville Academic Center for grades 3 to 8, and North Ridgeville High School on Bainbridge Road. Private options include Saint Peter School (K-8) and Lake Ridge Academy (K-12). A voter-approved bond issue in November 2013 paid for the replacement of the middle school, Elizabeth Wilcox Elementary and the Rangers Stadium, which opened for football in September 2016.

Commuters care about access. Highway access includes the Ohio Turnpike (I-80), the Outerbelt South Freeway (I-480), U.S. Route 20 and State Routes 10, 83 and 113. Lorain County Community College runs its University Partnership Ridge Campus in eastern North Ridgeville next to I-480. A University Hospitals branch operates locally, and the city hosts a Riddell Sports Group plant of 350,000 square feet that produces football helmets and pads.

Parks help listings too. The city lists Sandy Ridge Reservation, South Central Park, Frontier Park, Victory Park and Root Road Park among its recreation sites, and the annual Corn Festival, which grew from a 1975 bicentennial committee, is a local tradition you can mention in your listing description.

What city permits and rules matter before I sell in North Ridgeville?

Start with the Building Division, which issues permits, registers contractors and enforces zoning and property maintenance codes. Staff hold certification from the Ohio Board of Building Standards, and the division asks applicants to budget three weeks or more when plans need review. Each permit comes with a list of required inspections, and each one must be booked at least a day ahead.

The Planning and Zoning page explains that residential projects are checked for zoning compliance when the permit application arrives. Additions, decks, swimming pools, accessory storage buildings and fences are the common triggers. If a project does not meet the Zoning Code, the owner can bring it into compliance or ask the Board of Zoning and Building Appeals for a variance.

Before you list, walk the property and confirm that past work was permitted and closed out. Ask the Building Division whether an open permit or code notice is tied to your address, since a buyer's title search can surface it.

  • The city provides water, sanitary sewer and refuse and recycling collection to more than 13,900 accounts.
  • Sanitary sewer treatment is handled at the city-owned French Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant in Sheffield Village.
  • A stormwater utility was created by council ordinance in 2018, with the base rate set in 2019 and provisions for annual increases (Chapter 1058 of the city's codified ordinances).

How does the deed transfer work in Lorain County?

A sale of a North Ridgeville house is completed at the Lorain County Auditor, which stamps the deed and collects the conveyance fee before the document goes on record. The Real Estate Department takes transfers in person or through an approved e-file vendor, Monday through Thursday only. E-filed transfers are cut off at 3 p.m., and walk-in transfers at 4 p.m.

The auditor states that mail-in transfers ended on November 1, 2012, that handwritten forms are refused, and that incomplete forms or wrong fees come back unprocessed. Staff may not fill in forms or advise on legal questions, so a closing agent or lawyer normally files for you.

Three Ohio statutes shape the paperwork. Section 5302.30 obliges most owners of small residential buildings to give buyers a condition disclosure. Section 319.202 demands a sworn statement of value and assigns the conveyance fee to the seller. Section 322.02 allows a county to layer on its own transfer tax, with a ceiling of 30 cents for every hundred dollars of value, payable by the grantor ahead of recording. The auditor's website carries a conveyance fee calculator.

How do property taxes affect a North Ridgeville sale?

The Lorain County Treasurer bills North Ridgeville property in two halves, and the settlement sheet divides the amount owed with the buyer. Ohio bills run a year behind, so the one that arrives in your sale year pays for the year before. The treasurer's office sits in Room 201 of the Lorain County Administration Building in Elyria.

For 2026, the treasurer listed February 13 as the first-half due date and moved the second-half due date to July 31 because of House Bill 186, the inflation cap credit. Title and mortgage companies that print their own tax bills are exempt from duplicate bill fees. The treasurer also runs a monthly escrow plan for owners who like to spread the bill out.

Two county programs can matter to sellers. Owners who occupy the house as their residence on January 1 can apply for the 2.5 percent owner-occupancy reduction, which the auditor says is often arranged during the transfer. A valuation complaint to the county review board costs nothing and may be filed from the first of January through March 31, usually once per three-year cycle unless an exception such as an arm's length sale applies.

When does selling for cash fit a North Ridgeville house?

Cash works best when the calendar or the building's condition is the problem. Picture a probate house nobody wants to renovate, a rental the tenant is vacating, or a job transfer with a firm start date. The buyer accepts the flaws, so repairs, staging and the lender's appraisal drop out.

Judge any offer by what you would net from a listing, not the headline figure. Get the closing date in the contract, find out who covers the county conveyance fee and title charges, and ask whether open permits are acceptable. Declining costs nothing, so collect an offer next to your agent's price opinion.

More questions about North Ridgeville, OH

Which office handles the deed in a North Ridgeville sale?

The Lorain County Auditor's Real Estate Department, because the city lies in Lorain County. It accepts walk-in and e-filed transfers Monday through Thursday, and your closing agent or lawyer usually submits the right conveyance form.

Must I give a condition disclosure to North Ridgeville buyers?

Usually, yes. Section 5302.30 of the Ohio code asks owners of homes with up to four units to deliver the completed form promptly, and a buyer handed it only after signing gets three business days to back out. Transfers by an estate fiduciary, and some inherited homes you never lived in, are exempt.

Can I challenge my valuation before I sell?

You can try, within limits. In Lorain County, valuation complaints must be filed or postmarked by March 31, there is no fee, and normally allows one filing per three-year period unless the property sold at arm's length, was substantially improved or suffered casualty damage.

Does North Ridgeville inspect a house before it sells?

The city's building and zoning pages describe permits for construction work, and they do not describe a sale inspection. Ask the Building Division whether an open permit or code notice sits on your address, then close it out so the title search comes back clean.

How long does a cash sale in North Ridgeville take?

The contract decides. Because no lender appraisal is needed, the pace comes from title work and the closing date you negotiate. Spell out the date, the fee split and the as-is terms before you sign.

What sets Gahanna apart for a home seller?

Gahanna is a Columbus suburb with its own school district and its own downtown on the creek. Franklin County holds the city, which shares borders with Columbus on three sides, New Albany to the north, and Mifflin and Jefferson townships.

The name comes from a word for three creeks joining into one, and Big Walnut Creek, with its tributaries Rocky Fork Creek and Sycamore Run, still shapes the map. Gahanna and the neighboring village of Bridgeport merged under the Gahanna name, and the village was recorded as incorporated on August 8, 1881. A few small islands of Jefferson Township sit inside the city limits, so confirm with the Franklin County Auditor which taxing districts apply to your parcel.

Three practical items come up for sellers here: how rental registration affects a landlord's sale, what the county charges to transfer title, and how the creek system bears on a parcel.

How do Gahanna homes compare on the Census numbers?

Gahanna's figures run above the national ones in the same Census tables: a median owned-home value of $350,900 against $332,700 for the United States, household income of $109,061 against $80,734, and a bachelor's degree rate of 51.7 percent against 35.7 percent. Seven in ten households own their home.

Household makeup matters for what buyers want. A listing that shows a workable home office and room for children speaks to the households the numbers describe.

What does Gahanna require of a landlord selling a rental?

A rental owner needs to know the city's registration rules, because a buyer who keeps the property as a rental must register it within 30 days of the transfer. Gahanna's Ordinance 0053-2018 requires every residential rental owner to register every two years.

The city's rental registration page and its FAQ set out the details:

  • Registration runs between January 1 and March 15, and approved permits expire December 31 of the second year.
  • The fee table lists a $50 registration fee, plus a $100 permit fee for a single-family home or duplex.
  • Multifamily permit fees are $200 under 10 units, $400 for 10 to 59 units, $600 for 60 to 99 units and $800 for 100 or more.
  • Inspectors check the exterior from the sidewalk or right-of-way against the city codes and the International Property Maintenance Code, and no one has to be home.
  • Owner-occupied single-family homes (occupied more than half the year) may request an exemption case by case.
  • Airbnb-style rentals under 30 consecutive days count as short-term rentals and fall under the same program.

If tenants are in place when you sell, ask Code Enforcement whether any violations are open on the permit, since an unresolved report can slow a buyer's lender.

What does Franklin County charge to transfer a Gahanna deed?

The Franklin County Auditor bills $3 per $1,000 of price on a standard sale, split between a $1 state share and a $2 county share, and adds a $0.50 transfer tax. Use the Auditor's online calculator, which asks you to round the price up to the next $100 and applies a $3 floor.

The county share is waived when the seller holds the homestead exemption on the transfer date, which cuts the rate to $1 per $1,000. An exempt conveyance owes just the $0.50. The calculator page accepts cash, business checks and cashier's checks payable to the Franklin County Auditor and turns away personal checks, and the amount must be exact.

ORC 319.202 puts the statement of value on the buyer's side and makes the seller pay the fee. Value includes any mortgage or lien. The Transfer and Conveyance department answers questions at 614-525-3253.

Homestead status is worth checking before you sign. The Auditor FAQ says the standard credit goes to owners aged 65 by year-end or permanently and totally disabled, within an income cap, while disabled veterans at 100 percent can qualify for an enhanced credit with no income test.

Who are Gahanna's buyers and what draws them?

Gahanna uses ZIP code 43230 and the 614 and 380 area codes, and the city sits at about 794 feet of elevation on 12.43 square miles of land. It works as a commuter base: Interstate 670 and US 62 lead to John Glenn Columbus International Airport, Interstate 270 rings the area, Ohio 317 is the main north-south street through downtown, and COTA runs bus lines 24 and 25 through the center.

The Gahanna-Jefferson Public School District serves the city. According to Wikipedia, it runs seven elementary schools, three middle schools and Gahanna-Lincoln High School, and private options include Columbus Academy and Gahanna Christian Academy.

Downtown redevelopment has been part of the pitch since 2004. The Creekside project added a public park extension, restaurants, offices, residences and a 389-space garage. The city also runs a brownfields program with a community-wide inventory, assessments, and demolition of abandoned or environmentally suspect buildings. On the former Bedford I Landfill, a 200-acre cleanup became Central Park of Gahanna, home to a golf academy.

How does Gahanna's creek system affect a house sale?

Properties along Big Walnut Creek, Rocky Fork Creek and Sycamore Run deserve a flood and drainage check before listing, since the creeks have a significant effect on the local geography.

Ask the Franklin County Auditor's office or the city for the zone of your parcel, and keep any insurance, drainage or sump-pump records handy. A documented dry basement and a clear drainage path answer the question before a buyer raises it.

What are the options for selling a Gahanna house fast?

  • Agent listing: reaches mortgage-backed buyers, who will expect a clean inspection.
  • Direct sale: no commission, but you handle the disclosure form, DTE 100 and deed paperwork.
  • Investor purchase: useful when the home needs updating, a tenant is in place or you must close on a set date.

Ohio sellers of one-to-four unit homes complete the state disclosure form. Compare offers on the amount you take home after the conveyance fee, the tax proration and any loan payoff.

More questions about Gahanna, OH

Can I sell a Gahanna rental that is registered with the city?

Yes, registration does not stop a sale. A buyer who keeps it as a rental registers within 30 days after the transfer, and any open violation is best cleared first.

How much is the Franklin County conveyance fee on a Gahanna sale?

Standard sales run $3 per $1,000 plus the $0.50 transfer tax, and sellers with homestead at transfer pay $1 per $1,000. Run your price through the Auditor's calculator for the exact figure.

Where do I ask about homestead before a Gahanna closing?

The Franklin County Auditor's Homestead office handles it, at 373 S High St, 21st Floor, Columbus, or homestead@franklincountyohio.gov. Whether you hold it on the closing date decides the conveyance rate.

Which school district covers Gahanna houses?

Gahanna-Jefferson Public Schools, whose high school is Gahanna-Lincoln. Small Jefferson Township pockets sit within city limits, so verify the district for your address with the county.

Who pays the conveyance fee when a Gahanna house sells?

The seller pays under ORC 319.202, and the buyer files the statement of value. Your purchase contract may restate or shift it, so read the closing section.

Selling in Upper Arlington?

What should a seller check first in Upper Arlington?

Upper Arlington is a planned suburb on the northwest side of Columbus, and a sale there turns on lot layout, school boundaries and a handful of city rules that older houses trigger. The city lies entirely in Franklin County, with the Scioto River along its west edge and Columbus wrapping the north and east sides. The Census Bureau lists its land area at 9.79 square miles.

The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 35,893 people, a dip from the 36,800 recorded in 2020. What follows covers what the city inspects, what Franklin County handles and what Ohio expects from a seller on paper, so you can judge how quickly a sale can move.

How did Upper Arlington's planned layout shape its houses?

Two brothers who developed real estate bought the first 840 acres south of present-day Lane Avenue in 1913 and followed a Garden City plan with deep setbacks, parks and separate zones for shops and apartments. The place was called the Country Club District at first and carried the Upper Arlington name by 1917. The village incorporated in 1918, and cityhood came on February 8, 1941.

Annexation did the rest. Most of it came between the late 1940s and 1960, and the two largest, in 1954 and 1955, nearly doubled the city's area. Henderson Road has marked the northern edge since 1969. The result is two housing stocks on one map:

  • South of Lane Avenue, the Old Arlington district holds Colonial and English Revival houses. The district was added to the National Register in 1985.
  • North of Lane, post-war tracts such as River Ridge follow ordinary street grids with ranch houses, and the houses built from the 1960s on grew larger.

Which side of Lane Avenue your house sits on decides which city rules you run into first.

How costly is owning a home in Upper Arlington?

The five-year Census survey covering 2020 through 2024 paints a pricey, owner-heavy suburb. A buyer shopping here weighs your house against a high-priced local market, so condition and presentation carry weight.

  • About 79.4% of housing units are lived in by their owners.
  • The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $595,600.
  • Monthly ownership costs run $3,189 for households with a mortgage and $1,284 for those without.
  • The city holds 14,330 households averaging 2.52 people.
  • Household income at the midpoint is $155,167, and 79.8% of adults over 25 finished a four-year degree or more.
  • Roughly 88.2% of residents were in the same home twelve months earlier.

Workers commute 19.3 minutes on average, which suits a suburb a short drive from downtown Columbus and from the Ohio State campus east of the Olentangy River. The Upper Arlington City School District serves the whole city, and its high school was rebuilt in 2021.

Does the Old Arlington demolition rule affect a sale?

It can, if the buyer plans to tear the house down. In 2009 City Council adopted rules meant to discourage, without prohibiting, total demolition of historically significant homes. A six-month delay period gives owners and the city time to look for alternatives, and the rules appear in Articles 5, 6 and 7 of the Unified Development Ordinance.

The city's GIS maps show which properties are identified as historically significant, and Community Development posts a Guide to Demolition in the Historic District along with an owner statement and a demolition sign affidavit. If you are selling a house south of Lane Avenue to a builder or investor, tell the buyer up front and ask Community Development whether your parcel is flagged.

Which city offices handle permits and exterior complaints?

Community Development runs three divisions: Planning, Building and Code Compliance. The office at 3600 Tremont Road keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 5 pm, with 614-583-5070 as the main line and 614-583-5080 for inspections.

Exterior upkeep is mostly complaint driven. The city lists high grass and weeds, flaking paint, illegal temporary signs, excess lighting, trash and debris, and noise as common violations. A written Notice of Violation follows a confirmed complaint and sets a re-inspection date, which an officer may extend for substantial progress, bad weather or other mitigating circumstances. Most violations carry a maximum of $150 per offense per day, and a few are fourth degree misdemeanors with a $250 maximum fine and up to 30 days in jail.

What can you do with a cluttered or dated house before listing?

The city's own pages answer the practical questions. Bulk items go to the curb by 7 am on your regular collection day, and mattresses and box springs must be wrapped in plastic. Large appliances and anything containing Freon may cost extra, so ask Local Waste Services at 614-409-9375, option 2, before you set them out.

  • One garage or yard sale per residence is allowed in any six-month period, for no more than three consecutive days, with no permit.
  • A plumbing permit is needed to install or replace a boiler, water heater or water meter, or any time supply or waste lines change.
  • Decks, fences, driveway replacements, detached garages and pools each appear as their own permit type in the online system.

Finished basements, new decks and swapped water heaters are the usual places a permit gap shows up. Pull the permit history first and close any gap before you accept an offer.

How do rental registration and the value complaint work in Franklin County?

Because the whole city is in Franklin County, one auditor handles both topics. Landlords file owner or manager contact details with that office under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02, within 60 days of the notice that follows a property transfer or of receiving a tax bill. A property left unfiled draws a $150 fine for each tax year, and an owner living outside Ohio has to name an Ohio contact.

A value complaint also starts at the auditor. ORC 5715.19 sets the cutoff at the end of March after the tax year, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later, and the window for tax year 2025 shut on March 31, 2026. The board looks at the property's value only, so the tax bill itself is outside its scope.

Franklin's standard Homestead Exemption helps lower-income owners who turn 65 by year-end or are permanently and totally disabled. An enhanced version for veterans with a 100% service-connected rating shields $50,000 of appraised value from tax and has no income test.

What must an Ohio seller hand to the buyer?

Ohio's residential disclosure statute, section 5302.30, has the seller complete a state form about the condition of the property and pass a signed copy to the buyer early. If it arrives after the contract, the buyer gets a short window to back out, and that window also applies when the form never shows up.

Answer each item honestly and amend the form if facts change. Where you truly do not know an answer, the statute allows a good faith estimate.

How do you compare ways to sell quickly in Upper Arlington?

The trade is time against price. An agent listing puts the house in front of owner-occupant buyers, which means showings and waiting on a lender. A direct purchase as-is can shorten the wait, and the offer is lowered by whatever repairs the buyer absorbs.

  • Get each offer in writing with the closing date, who covers closing costs and which repairs are excluded.
  • Request proof of funds before you sign.
  • Look up the permit history and any open exterior complaint before listing, since both can push a closing date.

More questions about Upper Arlington, OH

Does Upper Arlington require a permit for a deck or fence?

Yes. Decks and fences each appear as residential permit types in the city's online system. Call Community Development at 614-583-5070 before work begins and confirm that earlier projects on your house were closed out.

Can a buyer tear down my Old Arlington house?

Often yes, after a delay. The 2009 rules in the Unified Development Ordinance set a six-month delay period for total demolition of historically significant homes. Ask Community Development whether your parcel is identified in the city's GIS maps.

Do I need to register a rental house in Upper Arlington before selling it?

The registration comes from the county auditor, not the city, and rests on Ohio Revised Code 5323.02. A missing filing carries a $150 fine per tax year, so update the contact record before closing. The auditor's line is 614-525-4663.

When can I dispute my home's value?

File with the Franklin County Auditor by the end of March after the tax year, or the first-half collection deadline when that is later. The Board of Revision, at 614-525-3913, rules on value only.

Who completes the Ohio property disclosure form?

The seller does. Section 5302.30 covers most sales of homes with up to four units, and some transfers, such as gifts to a spouse or a relative in the direct line, fall outside it.

How can you sell a house fast in Mason, Ohio?

Mason owners usually weigh a broker, a self-run sale and an as-is cash purchase. The county work after a contract is the same for all three, and it runs through Warren County's auditor and recorder.

Speed is the main trade. A traditional listing can attract many buyers, yet it also invites inspection credits, staging effort and weeks of showings. A direct cash sale skips most of that and lets you pick a closing date.

  • With an agent, you pay a commission and work through repair requests.

What do the numbers show about Mason homes and households?

Mason's median owner-occupied home is valued at $426,200 for 2020-2024, and owners live in 80.1 percent of the housing. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 35,834 people, 3.0 percent over the 2020 base.

QuickFacts lists median household income at $125,401 and median gross rent at $1,760. Education runs high, with 60.4 percent of adults 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree or more, and 17.1 percent of residents are foreign-born. The city counts 13,502 households of 2.60 people on average.

The city covers about 19 square miles, and the Little Miami River forms a short stretch of its border. The Weather Channel's averages list 44.68 inches of precipitation in a year, July highs near 87 degrees and January lows near 19, so roofs and gutters work through a full range of seasons.

How did Mason grow into a Warren County city?

Mason began as farmland: in 1803 William Mason paid $1,700 at auction for 640 acres in what is now downtown, and in 1815 he platted 16 lots and named the village Palmyra. Postal confusion with another Ohio Palmyra led to the name Mason in 1835.

For well over a century it stayed small. Main Street was paved in 1923, and in 1970, a year before Mason incorporated as a city, fewer than 5,700 people lived there. By the 2020 census the count was 34,792, and in 1997 the city separated from Deerfield Township to form a paper township named Mason Township.

One landmark from the early years still shapes the skyline: the WLW radio tower on Tylersville Road, built in 1928.

Which employers and attractions affect Mason buyers?

Corporate employers anchor the local economy. Cintas is headquartered in Mason, along with the Procter & Gamble Mason Business Center and the headquarters of Luxottica Retail, and more than 90 companies operate headquarters or manufacturing sites across the city's 24 commerce parks.

Kings Island amusement park and the Lindner Family Tennis Center, home of the Cincinnati Open, also sit in Mason. The city is about 22 miles north of downtown Cincinnati, and Sinclair Community College runs a 75-acre campus near I-71.

  • Seven city parks cover about 300 acres, with lakes, trails and ball fields.
  • The Mason Community Center, opened in 2003, covers 199,000 square feet with two pools and a senior center.
  • The Mason Municipal Center, a 120,000-square-foot building that opened in 2002, houses the municipal court, police and fire departments.

Which public schools serve Mason?

Mason City Schools serves the city with five public schools: Mason Early Childhood Center for pre-K through second grade, Mason Elementary for grades 3 and 4, Mason Intermediate for grades 5 and 6, Mason Middle for grades 7 and 8, and William Mason High School.

The last of these buildings to open was Mason Elementary, in 2019. Families often ask about the district before anything else, so put the school names on your listing sheet or give them to a cash buyer who plans to resell.

What does a deed transfer cost in Warren County?

On a Mason sale, Warren County's auditor charges a $1.00 state conveyance fee plus a $2.00 county levy for each $1,000 of price, a $3.00 combined rate. Each parcel carries a further $0.50 transfer fee, and cents in the total round up to the next dime.

The grantor pays at presentation, and the auditor endorses the deed once the money is in.

What paperwork does Warren County require on a Mason deed?

Every Warren County deed travels with DTE Form 100, the statement of value, or DTE Form 100EX when the sale is exempt, and fees are made out to the county auditor. The map department initials the deed first.

  • The grantor's name must read the way the grantor took title on the previous deed.
  • The prior deed reference of record must appear on the new deed.
  • If the land is in the farm-use valuation program now or was last year, DTE Form 102 must accompany the deed.
  • The grantor signs every Ohio deed, and a notary must acknowledge it.

Exemption reasons (b), (g) and (m) on the 100EX form require a notarized affidavit explaining why no money changed hands.

Which Mason projects need permits before closing?

Mason's Engineering, Building and Planning Department handles permits through an online portal, and it can be reached at 513.229.8520. Applications cover residential building and electric work, decks, pools and spas, fences, solar, demolition, retaining walls, sewer tap-ins and signs, as well as zoning certificates.

Ask the department about any open permits or completed work without a final inspection. Unfinished permits can stall a conventional sale, and a cash buyer will usually discount for them. A zoning certificate also answers whether a property is zoned for the use a buyer has in mind.

What should a Mason rental owner file after a sale?

Landlords owe the Warren County Auditor a contact filing on each rental parcel, and the statute (Ohio Revised Code 5323.02) gives 60 days to update it after a change. Expect the new owner to make that filing after the deed is endorsed.

If you are selling a rented house, agree in the contract on who handles deposits, the lease and move-out dates, and keep copies of what you give the buyer.

When does a cash offer suit a Mason seller?

Some Mason sellers want a short timeline instead of a long listing, and a cash sale can suit them. Examples include:

  • Owners relocating for a job on a deadline.
  • Heirs who have inherited a house and live elsewhere.
  • Sellers of a home that needs work that would cost more than they want to spend.

Ask for any offer in writing and set it beside a realistic listing net.

Who pays Warren County's deed fees on a Mason sale?

The seller, as grantor, pays them when the deed is presented to the auditor. Section 319.202 of the Ohio code charges both amounts to the grantor.

Does the Mason seller need to sign anything before the deed is accepted?

Yes. Under Ohio Revised Code 5301.01 the seller's signature on the deed needs a notary's acknowledgment, or that of another listed officer. Warren County also asks that the grantor's name match the previous deed.

Is a property disclosure form required in Mason?

Yes for houses of one to four units, with several exceptions. The form must be completed and handed to the buyer, and exceptions include estate transfers and relatives in the direct line.

What is the DTE 100EX form used for?

It states why a transfer is exempt from the conveyance fee. The buyer or the buyer's representative completes it, picks one of the listed reasons, and signs and dates it.

Where do I call about permits in Mason?

Call the city's Engineering, Building and Planning Department at 513.229.8520. Applications and permit fees are handled through the city's online permit portal.

Fairborn is a suburb of Dayton in the Dayton metropolitan area, and the county seat is Xenia. The Greene County Auditor handles the deed transfer for a Fairborn sale.

Wright State enrolls nearly 12,000 undergraduate and graduate students, and the median resident of Fairborn was 34.0 years old at the 2020 census, well below the other cities in this guide. That younger population shapes which homes move easily and which rentals turn over often.

How did Fairborn become one city out of two villages?

Fairborn is a combined name made from Fairfield and Osborn, the two villages that merged under a charter signed on January 1, 1950, with incorporation on August 1, 1950. Fairfield was founded in 1816 and Osborn in 1850, the latter named for a railroad superintendent whose line the village welcomed after Fairfield refused it.

After the Great Dayton Flood of 1913, the state created a conservation district here, and Huffman Dam went up on the Mad River in the 1920s. About 200 Osborn houses were moved by mules and tractors, and many still stand in the Historic Osborn District. From 1950 to 1970 the city grew to six times its former size, passing Xenia as the most populous city in Greene County, largely on the strength of the nearby Air Force base. Interstate 675, finished in 1987, now carries traffic along the east side of town.

Fairborn covers 14.725 square miles, with 8.864 square miles of the land zoned residential. The city manages 773.2 acres of parks, preserves and cemeteries, and Oakes Quarry Park is among its best known. Fairborn City Schools opened a new primary school in 2020, a new intermediate school in 2022 and a new high school in 2024, and the middle school is Fairborn Baker Middle School. Southwestern Portland Cement once ran the largest factory in the city, mining the locally exposed Brassfield Formation, and the Mercer Log House, 5/3 Commons, Central Park and the Wright Brothers Huffman Prairie Bikeway are among the places buyers hear about.

Census Bureau QuickFacts estimates Fairborn's population at 35,754 on July 1, 2025, a 3.7 percent rise from the 2020 base, which makes it the fastest growing of the four cities in this guide. The 2020 to 2024 median value of an owner occupied home is $175,000, and 51.2 percent of homes are lived in by their owners.

Which Fairborn city rules matter for a house sale?

Fairborn enforces a property maintenance code found in Part Thirteen, Title Five of its codified ordinances. It covers siding, broken windows, gutters, roofs, walls, foundations, sidewalks, sheds, garages, fences and debris, and it also reaches stored materials and vehicles parked in the yard. A violation notice on your address can complicate a closing, so deal with it early.

Fairborn also hosts the disaster training facility known as Calamityville, and growth since the late 1980s has run at a moderate pace, with neighboring Beavercreek now larger.

How does the Greene County Auditor handle a Fairborn deed?

Fairborn lies in Greene County, so the Greene County Auditor's office transfers the deed and charges the transfer and conveyance fees. The Real Estate Department can be reached at (937) 562-5072 and maintains records on more than 73,000 parcels.

A buyer who receives the form after signing may rescind within three business days, and no later than the earlier of 30 days after acceptance or closing.

Is a quick sale the better call for a Fairborn rental or inherited house?

A quick sale often fits a rental with a turnover problem or an inherited house with a distant owner. The state disclosure statute exempts a seller who inherited the property and did not live in it during the prior year, which removes one task from the list.

Before you sign with anyone, gather these items:

Call the city's 24 hour hotline at 937-318-1605. Parking and noise complaints go to the Fairborn Police Department non-emergency line at 937-754-3000.

Can a Fairborn buyer find out about assessments on a parcel?

Yes. The Finance Department accepts an Assessment Inquiry Form from people considering a purchase, and a representative responds with the assessment details.

Is the Fairborn income tax rate the same after a move out of the city?

No. The city levies a 2.0 percent income tax and a 0.5 percent school district tax on residents, so a move to another municipality can change what you owe. Ask a tax preparer about your situation.

Every sale runs through the same county sequence of engineer, auditor and recorder. Learning that order ahead of time keeps the closing date from slipping. A cash buyer cannot skip those stamps either, though it can reduce the lender-driven steps around them.

  • Pull together the deed, the latest tax bill and any payoff letters before speaking with buyers.
  • Learn which school district covers the address.

Where is Marion and what is the land like?

Marion lies about 50 miles north of Columbus along U.S. Route 23 on a flat glacial till plain. Ice melted in place here 12,000 to 14,000 years ago, leaving productive farm soils, and two small glacial lake plains sit to the west of town.

Settlers platted the city in 1822 and honored General Francis Marion in its name, and the Legislature incorporated it as a village during its 1829 and 1830 session. Its land area is 12.96 square miles with roughly 2,777 residents per square mile in 2020.

What industries built Marion and what employs people now?

Marion was a heavy equipment town. The Marion Steam Shovel Company, later Marion Power Shovel, built machines used on the Panama Canal and Hoover Dam, and in 1911 about 80 percent of the nation's steam shovels were made here. Later it produced the crawler-transporters that carried Saturn V rockets to the launch pad.

CSX and Norfolk Southern rail lines, one of the country's larger intermodal freight facilities and a handful of plants carry the economy. Whirlpool runs what is described as the world's largest clothes dryer factory, making over 20,000 dryers a day, and Nucor's Marion mill is Ohio's largest producer of rebar and signposts. Nucor announced an $85 million modernization in March 2017, and POET said that year it would spend $120 million to double its ethanol capacity.

The city promotes itself as America's Workforce Development Capital. Tri-Rivers Career Center, Marion Technical College and Ohio State University at Marion all sit in town, and Tri-Rivers hosts a robotics and advanced manufacturing training program called RAMTEC.

Who is likely to buy a Marion house?

Buyers here weigh monthly costs closely. Census data for 2020 to 2024 show median owner costs of $1,084 with a mortgage and $462 without one, against median gross rent of $856, so a modest house can compete with renting.

Households average 2.43 people, the largest figure among the four cities in this set, and 84.8 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Mean travel time to work is 21.0 minutes, and 2,282 residents are veterans. Landlords, first-time buyers and workers at the plants all appear in that mix, which is why a plain, working house with a sound roof and furnace sells in this market.

Which schools and roads serve Marion?

Most of the city belongs to the Marion City School District, which runs six elementary schools, a middle school and Marion Harding High School. Parts of the city fall in the Elgin, Pleasant, Ridgedale and River Valley local districts, so two houses a few blocks apart can have different schools.

U.S. Route 23 runs along the eastern edge of the city between Columbus and Findlay, and Ohio routes 4, 309 and 423 pass through. The Marion Municipal Airport is about 3.5 miles northeast of the central business district. A parochial school, St. Mary's, serves kindergarten through eighth grade.

A buyer will often ask which school building serves a house, so ask the district for the answer by address and avoid guessing from the street name.

How does a deed get transferred in Marion County?

Marion County describes three stops in a fixed order. The engineer's office goes first, comparing the legal description with its records and stamping approval, and that approval is good for 60 days.

Next comes the auditor, who needs a signed conveyance form and payment before processing, then stamps the deed as transferred. The auditor's calculator page states the conveyance fee as $4.00 per $1,000 of the total sale price and a 50 cent line fee for each parcel. The recorder is last and checks that the deed is properly executed and carries both stamps. Its recording fee is listed, effective October 17, 2019, at $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 for each additional page.

  • Engineer: legal description check and approval stamp.
  • Auditor: conveyance form, fees and transfer stamp.
  • Recorder: execution check, recording and return of the original.

The county posts the steps on its transferring property page. Call each office to confirm its present fees ahead of closing.

Which city offices matter to a Marion seller?

Marion's building department is new and its posted guidance, issued February 1, 2026, is organized around commercial permits and the Ohio Building Code. For a house repair, call the department at the number on its site and ask what applies to residential work.

Code enforcement sits in the police department. The officer there deals with junk motor vehicles and tires left in the public right-of-way and works with local tow companies, and posted weekday hours run Monday through Thursday, excluding holidays. An abandoned car or a pile of tires can draw a complaint, so clear the yard before listing.

The city's Contact Us page lists the police records bureau and the code enforcement phone line. Ask the city whether a complaint is open on your address before you sign a purchase contract.

What Marion landmarks and culture can help a listing?

The Palace Theatre, opened August 30, 1928 and restored in 1975, seats 1,440 and is one of only 16 remaining atmospheric theatres designed by John Eberson that still operate. A U.S. president lived in Marion and is buried here, and the city holds a number of historic properties of its own.

The Marion Public Library is the main public library, and the library at the OSU Marion campus holds over 48,000 books. In the 1800s the city was a stop on the route Ohioans call the River to Lake Freedom Trail, part of the Underground Railroad.

More questions about Marion, OH

What is the Marion County conveyance fee?

Use the transfer fee calculator on the Marion County Auditor's website, which applies the county's current rate and line fee to your sale price. Under Ohio law the seller, as grantor, pays it.

How long does the engineer's transfer stamp last?

Sixty days. After the engineer stamps the deed for transfer, finish the auditor and recorder steps inside that window or start the engineer step again.

Which school district is my Marion house in?

Most addresses fall in the Marion City School District. Others sit in the Elgin, Pleasant, Ridgedale or River Valley local districts, so verify the exact district with the schools before you advertise it.

Who handles junk cars or tires on a Marion property?

Marion's police department employs a code enforcement officer for those complaints. The phone number and weekday hours are on the city's Contact Us page.

Can I sell a Marion house with mortgage or lien problems?

Yes, provided the payoff is settled at closing. Ask your lender for a payoff letter and have a title company search for other liens, because the Recorder checks that the engineer and auditor stamps are on the deed.

The division reports that its inspectors completed over 1,300 property maintenance inspections in a recent year, and its reference list covers the Ohio building, plumbing, and mechanical codes, the National Electrical Code, and Brunswick's own ordinances. Staff register building contractors, issue permits, schedule inspections, and check storm water runoff and sediment control to meet Ohio EPA requirements. Permit applications and contractor registrations can be left in a drop box in the City Hall vestibule that the city says is open around the clock.

Several transfers are exempt, including those by an estate fiduciary and by an heir who did not occupy the house.

Which buyers shop for houses in Brunswick?

The 2020 census recorded 14,714 housing units in Brunswick, with 3.6% vacant, and 14,187 households. The median age was 41.5, with 21.4% of residents below 18 and 18.0% at 65 or above. About 29.5% of households included children under 18, and 52.7% were married-couple households.

So the typical buyer is a family or a couple already living in the Medina and Cleveland area. In the 2020-2024 survey period, 93.0% of adults held a high school diploma and 27.9% held a bachelor's degree. Households average 2.42 people, and 4.7% of residents were born abroad. The city covers 13.031 square miles with a density near 2,699 residents per square mile. Public students attend six elementary schools, one middle school, and Brunswick High School in the Brunswick City School District. Catholic families have St. Ambrose School, which covers kindergarten through eighth grade.

Cuyahoga Community College opened the Brunswick University Center in 2011 as an extension of its Western Campus. A branch of the Medina County District Library is in the city. The Census lists 2022 retail sales of about $1.27 billion, or $35,934 for each resident, so shopping is a real part of the local economy.

Where do I turn in a permit application in Brunswick?

Use the gray metal drop box in the City Hall vestibule at 4095 Center Road, which the city says is open around the clock. Calling 330-558-6830 first to book an appointment is the easiest route, since permits are never issued the same day.

Who enforces property maintenance rules on a Brunswick house?

The city's Building Division, through its property maintenance and zoning inspectors. Ask them whether a complaint is open on your address, because an unresolved item can surface during a sale.

Allen County's government sits in Lima, a northwest Ohio city that was platted in 1831 and takes its name from the capital of Peru. The city covers roughly 13.6 square miles of land at an elevation near 883 feet, with the Ottawa River crossing it.
