At the 2020 census Troy had 11,859 housing units, 5.6 percent of them empty. Children under 18 are 25.7 percent of residents, and the mean commute is 21.6 minutes.

Which Troy schools do buyers look at?

Most of Troy belongs to Troy City Schools: the high school covers grades 9 to 12, the junior high grades 7 and 8, and the elementary buildings are Concord, Cookson, Forest, Heywood, Hook, Kyle and Van Cleve. A slice of the city falls in the Miami East Local School District, so verify the district for your exact address before you advertise it.

Private options include Troy Christian (Pre-K to 12), St. Patrick School for kindergarten to 8 and Miami Montessori School. The Troy-Miami County Public Library has three locations in the city.

How do Troy's property maintenance and zoning rules affect a sale?

The city enforces the International Property Maintenance Code on existing homes and other structures, and ignoring it can bring penalties from the courts. Property maintenance staff log complaints and also find problems themselves. Troy publishes an exterior checklist, and walking your property with it before you list is an easy way to catch peeling paint, broken steps or overgrown yards.

If you added a shed, deck, garage or pool, ask the city's Planning and Zoning Division whether the zoning permit was finished, because a buyer's inspector or lender may ask for the paper trail.

What does Troy require about water service lines and utilities?

Troy houses built before February 1, 1944 could have lead water service lines, since the city banned lead in 1944. Because of the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule, the city is inventorying service line materials and mails owners of those homes a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is verified. A city technician can inspect in about 15 minutes on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. (937-335-4151), or you can self-report online.

On the buyer's side, the Utility Billing office at City Hall, 100 S. Market Street, opens an owner's service with photo ID plus a deed, closing papers or an accepted purchase contract. It also requires that any delinquency be resolved first, so settle your own account and call the office about the handover.

How does a Troy deed move through Miami County?

The standards Miami County adopted on August 12, 2025 set the sequence. The Engineer's office approves the instrument first. The Auditor then takes a completed DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100 EX exemption form, and the Recorder will file a deed only after it bears both approval stamps.

  • Seller names on the deed must match the previous deed, or an affidavit under Ohio Revised Code 5301.252 has to explain the gap in title.
  • A land contract needs Engineer approval and an Auditor date stamp before it is recorded.
  • Fee checks go to the Miami County Auditor for the exact amount, because overpayments are refused.
  • The Auditor's website offers a conveyance fee calculator that adds in the parcel transfer fee.

Ohio Revised Code 322.02 puts the county transfer tax on the grantor. The same standards cover next-of-kin affidavits, survivorship transfers and transfer on death affidavits, which matters when a Troy house comes from an estate.

When does a direct sale suit a Troy house?

It tends to fit three kinds of Troy property. The first is a pre-1944 house with an unverified water line and old systems. The second is a rental, since about 34.5 percent of occupied Troy homes are not owner-occupied. The third is an estate house where heirs live elsewhere.

In each case, ask the buyer in writing who handles the lead line inventory, any open permit and the county transfer paperwork, and keep a copy of the signed purchase contract for the utility office.

What does the Ohio disclosure statute say about timing?

Under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30, a buyer who first sees the property disclosure form after signing may rescind in writing within three business days of receipt. That right ends 30 days after acceptance or at closing, whichever is earlier. A buyer who received the form before making an offer has no rescission right.

So hand over the form with the first showing packet. A seller who inherited the house and did not live in it during the prior year is exempt.

More questions about Troy, OH

Where do I file a deed for a Troy house?

Miami County handles it. The Engineer approves the description, the Auditor processes the conveyance form, and the Recorder files the deed. Begin with the Engineer.

Does Troy have a historic district that limits changes?

Inside the overlay, yes: the Planning Commission reviews alterations. The district is generally bounded by the Miami River, Clay, Canal and Oxford streets, and Planning and Zoning can tell you if your address is in it.

Will an old Troy home need a lead service line inspection?

Only homes built before February 1, 1944 are in the inventory. Those owners receive a yearly letter until the line is replaced or its material is confirmed by inspection or self-report.

Who pays the conveyance fee when a Troy house sells?

You do, as grantor, under Ohio Revised Code 322.02. Run your sale price through the Miami County Auditor's online calculator, which includes the parcel transfer fee, before the closing date.

Can I sell a Troy house with unpermitted work?

Yes, though a buyer's inspector may ask about permits. Check with Planning and Zoning on any shed, deck or pool, and document or correct it before you list.

Wooster at a glance

Selling in Wooster?
We buy Wooster houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is Wooster like for a home seller?

Wooster is a Wayne County city of 27,115 people (Census Bureau estimate for July 1, 2025), and sellers here deal with higher prices than in the other cities Census QuickFacts lists beside it in the table below. The city takes its name from Revolutionary War general David Wooster, sits at about 1,135 feet above sea level along Killbuck Creek, and has roughly 17 square miles of land.

Population has barely moved in fifteen years: 26,119 in 2010, 27,232 at the 2020 census and 27,115 in the latest estimate. Wooster is an employer town as much as a residential one. Certified Angus Beef, Wooster Brush, Seaman Corp., Frito-Lay and LuK have operations or headquarters here, and the College of Wooster shares the city with two Ohio State campuses, the Agricultural Technical Institute and the Ohio Agricultural Research and Development Center.

Public schools belong to the Wooster City School District, which runs one preschool, four elementary schools, one middle school and Wooster High School. Confirm which building serves your address before you list.

How does the Wooster housing market compare with the rest of Ohio?

Wooster has the highest values among Wooster, Xenia, Youngstown and Zanesville, the four cities QuickFacts compares side by side. QuickFacts' 2020 to 2024 estimates put the typical Wooster home at $214,200 and the typical monthly rent at $918, against a household income of $66,898. Owners live in 65.2% of the homes. The same table lists $63,300 as the median value in Youngstown, so a Wooster seller is working with a very different price band.

  • Wooster counts 11,108 households of 2.11 people each, and the 2020 census found 37.3% of them were one person living alone.
  • About one resident in five (20.9%) is past 65, so estate and downsizing sales are a routine part of the market.
  • Bachelor's degrees: 36.9% of adults, the top rate among the four.
  • The average trip to work takes 17.4 minutes, the quickest of the four.

Short commutes and a college town feel help older houses near downtown, but they do not hide deferred maintenance. A buyer who needs a mortgage brings in an appraiser and an inspector, and either can reopen the price. Some owners skip that step by taking an as-is offer.

What does Wooster's property code program look for before a sale?

The city's Building Standards Division enforces the property maintenance and zoning codes on existing buildings, and it works through complaints plus systematic inspections of older neighborhoods. The division says it completes more than 1,000 inspections a year, and that complaint-driven inspections find a violation about 80% of the time while the targeted sweeps find one about 20% of the time.

When a violation is confirmed, an inspector contacts the owner and mails a letter, because the city deals with owners rather than tenants. If the issue is not resolved, the city can mow, haul debris or hire a contractor and then assess the cost to the owner, or refer the case for prosecution. The division reports that about 5 to 10 houses are demolished in Wooster in an average year.

These are the violations the division lists most often, and each is cheaper to fix before showings than after a buyer's inspector writes it up:

  • Weeds or grass above twelve inches (International Property Maintenance Code 302.4).
  • Rubbish or garbage piled outside or inside the structure (code 308.1).
  • Vehicles parked on lawns, tree lawns or sidewalks (Wooster Codified Ordinance 1169.10).
  • Peeling or flaking paint and unprotected exterior wood (code 304.2).
  • Roofs that admit rain and gutters or downspouts in poor repair (code 304.7).
  • Unlicensed or inoperable vehicles stored on the lot (code 302.8).
  • Cracked or broken window glass (code 304.13.1) and unsound decks or porches (code 304.10).

Permits, plan review and code complaints run through the city's online OpenGov system, which the division says it has used for paperless permitting since 2017.

How do Wayne County property taxes and value appeals work for a Wooster seller?

Valuation belongs to the Wayne County Auditor, whose office is at 428 West Liberty Street in Wooster, and collection belongs to the treasurer. An owner who disputes the value files a complaint with the Board of Revision between January 1 and March 31 for the tax year just ended. Complaints mailed must be postmarked by March 31, and email or fax filings must arrive by 11:59 p.m. that day.

The auditor's notice lists several rules that matter if a sale is close:

  • The complaint must be signed and notarized (Ohio Revised Code 5715.13).
  • An owner may file only one complaint per three-year cycle unless certain conditions are met. The current cycle covers tax years 2026, 2027 and 2028.
  • You still owe the first-half bill, and the second-half bill is not mailed until the complaint is resolved. If the board changes the value, any over- or underpayment is adjusted on the second-half bill.
  • Auditor staff cannot give legal advice, so consider an attorney for a complaint tied to a pending sale.

Before fixing a closing date, ask the treasurer's office what is owed on your parcel. The title company needs that figure to split the bill between you and the buyer.

Does farmland or a large lot change a Wooster house sale?

It can, because Wooster remains an agricultural center and some parcels around it may be enrolled in the Current Agricultural Use Value (CAUV) program, which lowers the tax bill on land kept in farm use. When land leaves agricultural use, Ohio Revised Code 5713.34 recoups the tax savings from the three tax years before the conversion and records the charge as a lien on the land.

The deed process also asks about this. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 builds a question into the deed paperwork. The buyer's value statement must either affirm that the seller said the land was not in the program or attach a sworn instrument saying it was, and only then does the auditor endorse the deed. Sellers of a house on several acres should call the Wayne County Auditor at (330) 287-5430 and ask whether the parcel is enrolled in CAUV or in an agricultural district, which runs for five years and carries a penalty for early withdrawal.

Which offices handle the common steps of a Wooster sale?

Most steps run through the city's Building Standards Division, the county auditor and the board of revision. The table lists where each task starts.

Where Wooster sellers start on common tasks
TaskOfficeWhat the page says
Property maintenance or zoning complaintCity of Wooster Building StandardsInspectors contact the owner first; the city may abate and bill the cost
Value complaintWayne County Board of Revision, 428 West Liberty StreetFile January 1 to March 31; notarized; one per three-year cycle
Farmland valuationWayne County Auditor, (330) 287-5430CAUV and agricultural district applications are filed with the auditor
Deed value statementWayne County AuditorGrantee files a value statement; the auditor endorses the deed (ORC 319.202)
Deed recordingCounty recorderFiled with the recorder for the parcel (ORC 5301.25)

What do Wooster buyers get within a short drive?

Wooster Memorial Park, known locally as Spangler Park, has about seven miles of trails along Rathburn Run, and Freedlander Park holds the city pool, basketball courts and a pond. Schellin Park has a skate park, and Christmas Run and Oak Hill parks offer pavilions and walking paths. The Alice Noble Ice Arena runs year-round, and the Secrest Arboretum sits on the research campus.

The cultural calendar leans on the college. The Ohio Light Opera performs at the College of Wooster, the Wooster Symphony Orchestra dates to 1915, and the Wayne Center for the Arts runs classes and exhibits. The Wayne County Fair fills each September. If your listing is near a park or the college, say so in the first lines of the description.

When does a cash offer make sense for a Wooster house?

Consider a cash offer if speed or condition outweighs the last dollar of list price. A Wooster listing means open houses, an inspection report and a lender's appraisal, and a violation letter from the city or a tired roof can stall each of them.

A direct purchase leaves the repairs to the buyer, which fits an inherited property, a rental with tenant trouble or a home with an open Building Standards case. Put every offer side by side, including who covers closing costs and the exact closing day, and read the settlement statement before you sign.

More questions about Wooster, OH

Can I sell a Wooster house that has an open code violation?

Yes, but disclose it to every buyer. Building Standards says it will agree on a workable timeline if an owner shows a plan, and that cases left unresolved are referred for prosecution. Many owners clear the violation before closing.

When can I appeal my Wayne County property value?

The window opens January 1 and closes March 31, and it covers the tax year just ended. For tax year 2026 that means January 1 through March 31, 2027. Expect a notary step and a limit of one complaint per three-year cycle.

Do I need a disclosure form for an inherited house in Wooster?

Often no. The statute excuses an estate's fiduciary and an heir who did not live in the house during the prior year. An heir who did live there should plan to complete the form.

What happens if my parcel is in the CAUV farm program?

A change away from farm use brings a charge equal to the savings over the three prior tax years (ORC 5713.34). Call the Wayne County Auditor before signing, so the contract says who pays it.

Who records the deed after a Wooster sale?

The Wayne County recorder files it after a notary or another listed official has taken the owner's acknowledgment and the auditor has endorsed the conveyance. The title company usually carries the paperwork through each step.

  • The median age was 45.0, and 21.3% of residents were 65 or older.

Long tenure means many sales come from a move toward family, a smaller home, or an inherited house that needs work. A seller who wants to close quickly has to pick between fixing the house first and selling it as is.

Does Lake Erie erosion affect an Avon Lake sale?

It does if the parcel lies inside a state-designated Coastal Erosion Area. The Ohio Department of Natural Resources says land in such an area has to be named on the state residential disclosure form when it sells, and a CEA permit comes first for a new building, a septic system, or a ground-level addition of 500 square feet or more.

The state's map viewer takes an address search. A heavy red line marks the landward edge of the area, and a data table lists measured recession in feet per year and the distance expected over the next 30 years if no further erosion control is added. Owners inside a designated area in Lorain, Erie, Ottawa or Lucas County may also qualify for the Erosion Control Loan Program.

Before listing a shoreline house, run its address through the viewer. If it falls inside the line, say so on the form and expect questions about shoreline work, past repairs and permits.

Which Avon Lake rules should a seller check?

The Avon Lake Building Department issues permits for buildings and structures, does the inspections tied to each permit, and enforces the Ohio Building Code and the Residential Code of Ohio. The online portal takes applications, and the office sits at 750 Avon Belden Road. Close out any permit with unfinished work before listing, because buyers' inspectors look for it. Office hours are weekdays from 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and a drop box at the entrance takes paperwork after hours and is emptied each weekday morning, which helps if you are finishing a permit while managing a move.

Vacation-style rentals get a separate program. Under Ordinance 25-161 an owner applies for certification, the city sends someone for a life safety inspection within 14 days, and the certificate lasts 12 months before renewal. The application asks for proof of insurance and of paid property taxes and utilities. Chapter 14 also keeps short-term rentals 1,000 feet apart, with a carve-out for properties already operating before the ordinance.

A house that has hosted short-term guests raises one question for Community Development: does the certificate pass to a buyer? Anyone planning to keep renting will want the answer before closing.

Which schools and parks come up when buyers shop in Avon Lake?

One district, Avon Lake City Schools, runs every public school in town: Eastview, Erieview, Redwood and Westview elementaries (kindergarten to grade 4), Troy Intermediate (grades 5 and 6), Learwood Middle (7 and 8) and Avon Lake High. St. Joseph's, a parochial school, serves kindergarten through eighth grade.

Parks add to the draw. The city sets aside about 220 acres for parks and playgrounds, operates six community parks (among them Bleser Park, Miller Road Park and Veterans Memorial Park), and rebuilt the Ellen Trivanovich Aquatic Center in 2010. Neighborhood parks such as Belle Road, Inwood, Overlook, Resatar and Sunset connect by bike trail.

What do Lorain County offices require for a deed and tax bill?

An Avon Lake deed is transferred at the Lorain County Auditor's office in Elyria. Its Real Estate Transfers page rules out mail: conveyances arrive in person or through an approved e-file vendor. Handwritten forms are refused, anything incomplete or short on fees is returned, and staff may not advise on the forms. A title company or attorney usually does the filing.

Title and mortgage companiesExempt from duplicate bill fees if they print their own bills

Sources: loraincountyauditor.gov and loraincountytreasurer.gov.

Because the state can change the schedule, ask the treasurer's office which dates govern the year you close. On the deed itself, ORC 5301.01 calls for the seller's signature to be acknowledged before a notary or similar official, and ORC 5301.25 makes recording with the county recorder the buyer's shield against later claims.

How should an Avon Lake owner weigh a cash offer against listing?

A listing can pay the most when the house shows well and you can sit through showings and an appraisal. A cash offer swaps some of that price for a fixed closing date and no dependence on a buyer's mortgage approval.

Whichever route you lean toward, have each buyer put the price, the closing date and the split of title and transfer costs on paper. Fill in the disclosure form early, with shoreline notes if they apply, and confirm no permit is open. Then set each offer next to a listing's likely net, after agent fees, repairs and the carrying costs of the weeks it takes.

More questions about Avon Lake, OH

Is my Avon Lake house in a Coastal Erosion Area?

Search the address in the ODNR Coastal Erosion Area map viewer. Property inside the area is named on the state disclosure form at sale, and a new building, a septic system or an addition of 500 square feet or more needs a CEA permit.

Does an Avon Lake seller have to fill out the state disclosure form?

Most do. ORC 5302.30 covers homes of up to four units, and it excepts estate fiduciaries, transfers to relatives and sales to a buyer who already lived there for a year.

Can a buyer keep running my Avon Lake short-term rental?

Ask the city first. Ordinance 25-161 certifies each short-term rental after an application and a life safety inspection, renewed every 12 months, so whether a new owner inherits the certificate is a question for Community Development.

How does a deed get filed with Lorain County?

Through the Lorain County Auditor in Elyria, in person or by e-file, with no mail accepted and every form typed and complete. A title company normally takes care of it at closing.

When are Lorain County property taxes due?

The treasurer posted February 13, 2026 for the first half and July 31, 2026 for the second half, which a state change had moved. The treasurer can tell you which dates apply to the year you close.

Xenia at a glance

Selling in Xenia?

What makes selling a house in Xenia, Ohio different?

Xenia is the Greene County seat, about 15 miles east of Dayton in the Miami Valley, and its housing history is shaped by storms. A tornado rated F5 crossed the middle of the city on April 3, 1974, during the Super Outbreak. It killed 34 people, injured 1,150, destroyed almost half of the city's buildings and left 10,000 people homeless. Another tornado hit on September 20, 2000, and was rated F4.

The city's own history menu still carries a page titled "Xenia Lives!" about the 1974 recovery, and the city keeps a system of tornado sirens. A seller who can hand a buyer receipts for a recent roof, siding or storm repair has useful paperwork, because storm history is an obvious question in Xenia.

Xenia's 2025 Census estimate is 26,425 people, a 3.8% gain on the 25,447 in the 2020 estimates base. That is the fastest growth of the four cities QuickFacts compares here.

What do Census numbers say about Xenia homes and owners?

The Xenia numbers sit between a college-town market and a heavily rental city. Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 gives the figures below.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 60.9%, with a median owner-occupied value of $162,400.
  • Median gross rent: $931, the highest of the four Ohio cities QuickFacts lists beside Xenia (Wooster, Youngstown and Zanesville).
  • 10,765 households averaging 2.32 people.
  • 22.4% of residents are under 18, and 20.4% are 65 or older.
  • Mean travel time to work is 24.6 minutes, the longest of the four. The city's website carries a page for people relocating to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
  • Median household income is $56,029, and 17.9% of residents are in poverty.

Wikipedia describes Xenia as centrally placed in a transportation triangle formed by I-70, I-71 and I-75, reached by U.S. 35, U.S. 42 and U.S. 68. A listing can state the highway access plainly, since buyers who drive to Dayton or beyond will check it.

Which Xenia schools and neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Xenia Community Schools serves the city with a preschool, five elementary schools (Cox, McKinley, Arrowood, Shawnee and Tecumseh), Warner Middle School and Xenia High School. Private options include Legacy Christian Academy and St. Brigid School. The Greene County Public Library has its main branch and administrative offices in the city.

Several city landmarks come up in showings. The Little Miami Scenic Trail runs through Xenia Station, and the city carries the nickname "Bicycle Capital of the Midwest," and five of its six former rail roadbeds have been converted to trail use. The Greene County Fairgrounds hosts the annual Dayton Hamvention, which Wikipedia says typically draws more than 20,000 amateur radio enthusiasts. If your house sits near the fairgrounds, mention the event traffic in your showing notes so buyers are not surprised.

How do Xenia zoning and property maintenance rules affect a sale?

Planning and Zoning issues zoning permits and also enforces the property maintenance code, the city's floor for safe, sanitary buildings. The division works from the City Administration Building at 107 East Main Street, weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m., and takes calls at 937-372-6389.

Two practical points for sellers:

  • The city's project list includes a "Zoning Update 2026." Ask Planning and Zoning whether the update changes the rules for your lot, an addition or an accessory building before you promise a buyer a particular use.
  • Code enforcement is a separate page on the city site from the Building Division. A notice about tall grass, debris or a failing structure is best answered before the house goes on the market.

The Planning and Zoning page sits under the city's Development Services Department, which is the place to start with a question about an unpermitted porch, deck or garage.

How does Greene County value a Xenia house, and when can you appeal?

The Greene County Auditor values property by mass appraisal, building a table from sales data in each area and testing it against actual sales. The auditor's FAQ notes that Ohio does not allow foreclosure sales in that analysis because they are not arm's-length sales, so a distressed sale next door should not drag your value down in the county's model.

A triennial update happens every three years without a visual inspection, and a full revaluation with a physical review happens in the sixth year. An owner who thinks the appraisal is too high may file with the Greene County Board of Revision, and the window runs January 1 to March 31. The auditor's FAQ also says there is no dollar-for-dollar link between a change in value and a change in taxes, because the voted levies are applied to the value.

Homestead rules and income limits change over time, so ask the Greene County Auditor for the current application and limits rather than relying on an old figure.

What happens to property taxes if a Xenia house is damaged by a tornado or fire?

Ohio gives the county board of revision a specific tool in Ohio Revised Code 323.17. If fire, flood, a tornado or another cause destroys or damages taxable property by 25% or more of its listed value, and at least $2,000 of taxable value, the board may pass a resolution pushing the payment deadline back by as much as a year.

Copies go to the auditor and treasurer along with the board's damage estimate. Owners selling a storm-damaged house should ask the Greene County Auditor how to request an extension and should tell the title company, so the settlement statement shows what remains unpaid.

Who handles the deed, recording and transfer fee in a Xenia sale?

Three offices touch a Xenia deed. A notary or another listed official takes the owner's acknowledgment (ORC 5301.01), the Greene County Auditor endorses the conveyance once the buyer files a value statement and the seller pays the conveyance fee (ORC 319.202), and the recorder then files it. A deed left unrecorded can lose to a later buyer who had no notice (ORC 5301.25).

When does a cash offer make sense for a Xenia house?

A cash offer suits a Xenia house that a lender's appraiser would mark down, such as one with worn shingles, a wet basement or storm repairs never finished. Owners who inherited a house or manage a rental from out of town also use it.

Get each offer in writing with the closing date and the party responsible for closing costs. Set the figures beside what a regular listing would net after commission and repairs, and ask the title company for a draft settlement statement early.

More questions about Xenia, OH

Does Xenia's tornado history change how I should sell?

It changes what buyers ask. The April 1974 F5 and the September 2000 F4 are well known, so keep receipts for roof, siding and storm repairs and hand them over early. The city also keeps a siren system, which some buyers ask about.

Does Greene County count a foreclosure sale when it sets values?

No. The auditor's FAQ says Ohio does not allow foreclosure sales in the county's analysis because they are not arm's-length sales. Ordinary sales in your area are what the appraisal tables are tested against.

Is my Xenia house covered by a tax extension if a tornado damaged it?

Possibly. Section 323.17 lets the Greene County board of revision grant up to a year more to pay when the loss reaches 25% of listed value and $2,000 of taxable value. Ask the auditor how to apply.

Where do I ask about zoning for a house in Xenia?

Phone Planning and Zoning at 937-372-6389 or stop by 107 East Main Street on a weekday between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Raise the Zoning Update 2026 project if the property has an addition or a second building.

How long can I wait to appeal my Greene County value?

The county takes complaints from January 1 until March 31 each year. The board looks at value only, so the voted levy rates stay as they are.

Pickerington at a glance

Selling in Pickerington?

Why is Pickerington split between two counties?

Pickerington straddles Fairfield and Franklin counties, so your tax bill, auditor and treasurer depend on which side of the line the parcel falls. Wikipedia ranks it as the second-largest city in Fairfield County after Lancaster, yet a Pickerington address can still be billed by Franklin County.

The city was founded in 1815 as Jacksonville, renamed in 1827 for Abraham Pickering, certified as a city in 1991, and named the Violet Capital of Ohio by the legislature in 1996, according to Wikipedia. It sits about 840 feet above sea level just east of Columbus. The July 2025 federal estimate is 26,333 people, 14.1% above the 2020 estimates base of 23,070. Look up your parcel number before listing so you know which county offices to call.

How would you describe Pickerington's housing stock and buyers?

It is a family suburb with high owner occupancy and a high price point. Owners occupy 76.8% of homes in the 2020 to 2024 QuickFacts table, with a $339,600 midpoint value and $1,605 midpoint rent. There are 8,420 households of 2.89 people on average, and children under 18 are 27.5% of the population.

  • Median household income is $111,833 and per capita income is $46,372.
  • Workers spend 26.9 minutes getting to their jobs, typical of a commuter suburb.
  • OhioHealth Pickerington Methodist Hospital became a full-service hospital in December 2023, a plus for buyers who want medical care close by.

Buyers who use a mortgage face an appraisal and a lender's review, so a house that needs repairs can stall in a retail sale, which is where as-is offers come in.

How do Pickerington schools affect where buyers look?

Buyers sort by the Pickerington Local School District, which Wikipedia describes as 15 buildings: two high schools, an alternative high school, two junior highs, three middle schools, seven elementary schools and an early childhood center. The two main high schools are Pickerington High School Central and Pickerington High School North.

Elementary names in the district include Fairfield, Heritage, Pickerington, Violet, Tussing, Sycamore Creek and Toll Gate. When you write a listing, name the school buildings that serve the street, because families often search by building. Ask the district office to confirm attendance zones before you advertise them, since boundaries can change.

How has Pickerington grown, and what does the housing count show?

The city grew from 18,291 people in 2010 to 23,094 in 2020, and Wikipedia credits annexation, development and in-migration tied to Columbus. In 2020 it had 7,914 households and 8,373 housing units, 5.5% of them vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.3% and the rental vacancy rate 13.3%, so empty owner-occupied houses are scarce while rentals sit open more often.

The median age was 35.5 in 2020 and 44.8% of households had children under 18. Newer subdivisions, the Olde Pickerington Village core and the Motorcycle Hall of Fame off Interstate 70 give the city several different faces, so describe the part of town your house sits in rather than the whole city.

What permits and codes apply to a Pickerington house?

The city Building Department reviews plans, issues permits and inspects structures, and it is certified by the Ohio Board of Building Standards to enforce the 2019 Residential Code of Ohio and the 2024 Ohio Building Code. Contractor registration and building permits are filed on the city's OpenGov portal.

If past work on the house, such as a deck or finished basement, was done without a permit, sort it out before a buyer's inspector asks. Code Enforcement answers questions at 614-833-2204.

How does Pickerington handle code complaints and vacant houses?

Code enforcement runs on complaints from residents, and the city lists examples such as grass above 6 inches on a developed lot, piled debris and structures that are not maintained. Property maintenance and junk vehicle cases can take up to a month of legal steps before the owner gets a summons to Mayor's Court.

Vacant and abandoned homes must be registered. The city lists an annual $150 fee, due January 1 and received no later than January 31, with no proration. The registration names the mortgagee and, for an out-of-area owner, the local property manager. A buyer of a bank-owned house is told to check lien information with the zoning officer. Owners are also responsible for clearing sidewalks and storm drains under Section 660.05 of the Pickerington Codified Ordinances.

How do Fairfield and Franklin County taxes work for a Pickerington seller?

Fairfield County states that taxable value is 35% of market value, and any levy above the ten-mill limit needed a vote. Franklin County parcels follow the same state system but are administered from Columbus. Call the Fairfield County Auditor at 740-652-7020 or the Franklin County Treasurer at 614-525-3438 for your parcel's dates before you pick a closing day.

Two Franklin County facts are on its Treasurer page: the second-half 2025 payment was due July 20, 2026, and appeals of 2026 property value can be filed with the Auditor from November 20, 2026 through March 31, 2027. For Fairfield owners, the Auditor's Homestead program exempts the first $29,000 of value for qualifying owners and wants a wet-signed application filed within the year. The credit does not follow a homeowner to a new house, so a seller moving within the area must apply again at the new address.

What should a Pickerington owner do first when a quick sale is the goal?

Start with the paperwork that only you can fix, then decide how to sell. A few checks save days later.

  • Find the parcel number and confirm whether Fairfield or Franklin County bills it.
  • Ask the Building Department about any permit that was never closed for a deck, basement or addition.
  • Check whether a vacant house still needs its annual $150 registration and whether a lien exists.
  • Find out if you hold a Homestead credit, since Fairfield County says it does not transfer to a new home.
  • Gather the school names that serve the street, the age of the roof and furnace, and any HOA rules.

With those answers in hand, a listing agent, a direct buyer or the county offices can each respond faster, and you can compare offers on the same facts.

Which Pickerington fees and dates are worth writing down?

Who should consider a cash sale in Pickerington?

Cash suits a seller who values a firm closing date over squeezing out extra price. At these values a lender will require an appraisal, and a buyer's inspection can reopen the price when the roof is old or a deck lacks a permit.

Direct buyers usually take the property in current condition, a help with an inherited house, a rental after a tenant leaves or a vacant house that needs registering. Request written offers from more than one buyer and ask who pays closing costs.

More questions about Pickerington, OH

Who bills property tax on a Pickerington house?

It is Fairfield or Franklin County depending on the parcel, since the city spans both. Look up your parcel number and ask that county's treasurer for the due dates.

Does Pickerington require me to register a vacant house?

Yes. The city requires registration of abandoned or vacant homes with an annual fee of $150, due January 1 and received by January 31 each year.

How big is the Fairfield County Homestead exemption?

Qualifying owners can exempt the first $29,000 of appraised value, according to the Fairfield County Auditor. The form needs a wet signature and must be filed within the year the credit is sought.

Can I sell a Pickerington house with an unpermitted deck?

You can, but a buyer's inspector may find it. The Building Department explains the permit steps, and a direct buyer may take the house as is.

Sell Your Medina House for Cash

Medina at a glance

Selling in Medina?
We buy Medina houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How do you sell a house fast in Medina, Ohio?

A Medina owner can hire a broker, go it alone, or accept an offer that buys the house in its current state. Each version ends with a deed at the Medina County Auditor and a filing at the recorder.

Time and condition usually decide the choice. A listing can draw several offers, but it also brings showings, inspection findings and a contract tied to the buyer's loan. A cash purchase narrows the process to one conversation about price and closing date.

  • List with an agent: broader reach, plus commission and repair negotiations.
  • Go it alone: you set the price and run the process.
  • Sell for cash: one negotiated offer for the house in its current state.

How do Medina's Census numbers read for homeowners?

Medina's population is estimated at 25,692 on July 1, 2025, down 1.5 percent from a 2020 base of 26,075. Owner-occupied homes have a 2020-2024 median value of $243,600, and owners live in 67.3 percent of units.

Median gross rent is $1,077 and median household income is $77,385. Households number 10,911 at 2.33 people apiece, and 92.1 percent of residents stayed in the same home over the prior year. Of residents 25 and older, 35.6 percent hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

Land area is 11.58 square miles, so the 2020 count works out to 2,252.8 residents per square mile, and the grid around the Square is tight.

How does Medina's past show up in its houses?

Medina's center is a historic district, so older homes near the Square sit in a place that works to preserve its look. A Community Design Committee and a Historic Preservation Board look after the historic character, and the district covers a nine-block area around Uptown Park.

The Square dates to rebuilding after two fires. An 1848 blaze destroyed the whole business district, and an 1870 fire destroyed 45 buildings, after which it took almost ten years to replace the buildings, which is why the Victorian style is so common there.

Medina milestones

Source: Wikipedia, Medina, Ohio.

Where is Medina, and which schools serve it?

Medina is about 33 miles south of Cleveland and 23 miles west of Akron, and the city has parts in Lafayette, Medina, Montville and York townships. Many residents commute to Cleveland and Akron, and RPM International is among the companies based in town. Workers spend a mean of 24.3 minutes getting to their jobs, per QuickFacts.

The Medina City School District serves the city. Its schools include Medina High School, A.I. Root and Claggett middle schools, and the elementary schools Ella Canavan, H.G. Blake, Sidney Fenn, Eliza Northrop and Ralph E. Waite. Garfield and Heritage elementary schools closed at the end of the 2023-24 school year after redistricting.

The Medina County Career Center serves 11th and 12th graders and adults, and the private options include St. Francis Xavier School and Medina Christian Academy.

What civic landmarks and local news serve Medina residents?

The Old Medina County Courthouse is among the city's landmarks, and the Medina County District Library has its main branch in town. Uptown Park anchors the center, and the nine-block historic district surrounds it.

The Medina County Gazette publishes every day except Sundays and federal holidays, and The Medina Post is a free weekly that comes out on Saturdays. Television and radio reach the city from the Cleveland, Akron and Canton markets.

The Medina County Career Center South Campus sits a quarter-mile south of the city and teaches adult courses in law enforcement, run with the Medina County Sheriff's Office, and in paramedic training.

What does Medina's Building Department regulate?

The city's Building Department handles plan review, inspections and property maintenance enforcement, and it tries to link owners of run-down properties with assistance programs and volunteer groups. You can reach it at 330-722-9030.

Ohio's 2024 Building, Mechanical and Plumbing Codes took effect March 1, 2024, and the department holds every application received after that date to those requirements. Ask the city's Planning Department any zoning questions about a lot or an outbuilding.

After a finished basement, a new deck or replaced mechanicals, ask the department whether the permits were closed out. A buyer's inspector will ask too, and a cash buyer will price any gap.

What does the Medina County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

Medina County's real property conveyance fee is $3.00 for every $1,000 of sale price, per the auditor. The auditor rounds a price up to the next $100 when it ends in a fraction, and an online calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The auditor's site separates taxable conveyances from exempt ones and posts a form for each. They include DTE 100 for value, DTE 100EX for exemptions and a statement for farm-use valuation land.

Ask the auditor how the current figure applies to your sale before you set a price.

Which Medina transfers are exempt from the conveyance fee?

The county lists more than two dozen exemption reasons, and several of them involve families and estates. Among them are transfers:

  • Gifts between spouses or between a parent and child.
  • To an heir or devisee, between spouses, to a surviving spouse, or on the death of a registered owner.
  • Transfers where nothing of value changes hands and no gift is involved.
  • To a trustee when the trust's grantor can revoke it freely.
  • Under a court order, to the extent the transfer is not a sale carried out under that order.
  • On sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.

An exempt transfer still needs paperwork. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 swaps the full value statement for a short statement of the exemption reason.

What happens if a Medina property is a rental?

A rental parcel needs a contact filing at the county auditor, with updates due 60 days after any change (Ohio Revised Code 5323.02). The auditor's endorsement on a rental deed points the new owner to that filing.

Mention the tenants and the lease in your first conversation with a buyer, and keep records of deposits and rent already paid.

When might a cash offer suit a Medina seller?

Cash tends to fit when the owner wants certainty more than the widest market. In Medina that can include owners with historic-district houses that need expensive work, heirs who live away, and landlords who want out of a rental.

  • Ask what is assumed: as-is, closing costs and move-out date.
  • Compare the figure to a listing net after repairs, commission and carrying costs.
  • Read the contract for who pays the conveyance fee and recording charges.

What kind of place is Avon, Ohio for a home seller?

Avon is a Lorain County suburb in the Cleveland area, and most of its homes are owner-occupied. The city has 20.79 square miles of land, nearly twice the area of neighboring Avon Lake, and Census estimates put it at 25,611 residents for 2025.

The land began as Township Number 7 in the Western Reserve, with its first permanent settlers arriving in 1814. The township was organized in 1818 as Xeuma, later became Troy Township, and took the name Avon Township when Lorain County formed in 1824. A post office opened in 1825, the area incorporated as a village in 1917, and it became the City of Avon in 1961.

Growth has been steady. Wikipedia's census table shows 11,446 residents in 2000, 21,193 in 2010 and 24,847 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 25,611 is about 3% above the 2020 base.

What do the Census numbers say about Avon homes?

Home values run high in Avon. In the 2020 to 2024 data, 88.3% of homes are owner-occupied and the median value is $395,900. The 9,502 households average 2.63 people, rent has a median of $1,796, and monthly owner costs come to $2,471 with a mortgage and $818 without.

  • In the 2020 census, 41.5% of households had children under 18.
  • Married couples headed 64.2% of households, and the median age was 40.7.
  • The city had 9,208 housing units, with 4.2% vacant.

Those figures describe buyers who expect a move-in ready house. A seller who cannot take on repairs, or who faces a divorce, a relocation or an estate, may find a direct purchase simpler than preparing the house for the open market.

The Lorain County Treasurer runs an optional monthly escrow plan for tax payments, and the treasurer's site posts the current due dates, which have moved when the state changed the schedule. Your title company will prorate the tax between you and the buyer.

Which Avon schools and amenities do buyers ask about?

Avon Local School District serves the city. Its buildings are the Early Learning Center for preschool and kindergarten, Avon East Elementary for grades 1 and 2, Heritage Elementary for grades 3 through 5, Avon Middle School for grades 6 through 8, and Avon High School. Avon Middle School was named a Blue Ribbon school for 2020 by the U.S. Department of Education. Private options the city lists include Holy Trinity School, St. Mary School and Avon Montessori Academy.

The library is a branch of the Lorain Public Library, and a 16,000 square foot expansion opened in January 2023. The city runs parks along Detroit Road and Schwartz Road, an aquatic facility, a senior center and a dog park, and the Lake Erie Crushers play on Baseball Boulevard. Trash goes out on Mondays with Republic Services, and the city handles fall leaf pickup. The Service Department clears snow on more than 250 lane miles in a set order of main, secondary and residential streets. Avon belongs to the Northeast Ohio Public Energy Council for gas and electric supply, which a household can stay with or leave.

What Avon rules affect a house you plan to sell?

The Avon Building and Zoning Departments share City Hall at 36600 Detroit Road. The city tells residents to contact the Building Department for a pool, irrigation, deck, patio, shed, finished basement, fence, new roof, siding or any addition, and says contractors must be registered. Avon runs on a mayor and council form of government, with seven part-time council members (three at large and four by ward). Work sessions are held on the first and third Mondays and regular meetings on the second and fourth Mondays at 7:30 p.m., so a seller who needs a zoning question aired in public knows when to attend.

  • Utilities: water and sewer bills go out monthly and are due on the 25th, and meters report actual daily use. Call the Utilities Department to move service out of your name.
  • Sprinklers: an in-ground system needs an approved backflow device, tested each year before June 30, with results sent to the city.
  • Short-term rentals: a 2021 ordinance extending a moratorium said the zoning code bars uses it does not list, and that short-term rentals are not listed. Ask the Zoning Department whether anything has changed before you market the house to an investor.

How does the Ohio paperwork work for an Avon seller?

Ohio law has the seller of a residence with up to four units complete the state disclosure form and deliver it to the buyer (ORC 5302.30). Estate fiduciary sales and transfers to relatives are among the exceptions. If the form arrives after the contract is signed, the buyer has three business days to cancel in writing.

The owner must sign the deed before a notary or another official listed in ORC 5301.01. The deed is then filed with the county recorder, and ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent against a later purchaser who did not know of it. Before recording, the deed passes through the Lorain County Auditor, which accepts conveyances only in person or by e-file, wants typed forms and returns anything incomplete. County staff cannot fill out the forms, so let the title company file them.

When is a cash sale the better choice in Avon?

A cash sale suits a seller who values a firm closing date over a top price. In a high-value suburb, a listing can draw strong offers, but it also brings staging, showings and repair requests from the buyer.

Work out the net from each route. Add agent fees, repair costs, mortgage payments, taxes and utilities for the weeks a listing may take, and set that total against a direct offer. Get the offer in writing with a closing date, and keep a copy of your signed disclosure form.

Who processes the deed for an Avon sale?

The Lorain County Auditor processes the transfer and the county recorder files the deed. The auditor takes conveyances in person or by e-file only, and a title company normally handles both steps.

Avon Schools received 66.43% of the 2025 tax year bill, according to the city's welcome packet. Lorain County received 19.18% and the city 10.12%.

Any permit for a deck, pool, shed, fence, roof, siding, finished basement or addition. Ask the Building Department at City Hall about open permits and unfinished inspections.

  • Selling alone works when a closing agent or a lawyer drafts the deed and the settlement sheet.

Where does Perrysburg come from, and what did that leave behind?

Perrysburg is a Wood County city on the south bank of the Maumee River, about 12 miles southwest of Toledo. Federal surveyors platted it in the summer of 1816, and the name honors Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry. Fort Meigs, begun in February 1813 on a bluff above the water, is the largest wooden walled fortification in North America, and two critical battles with the British took place there during the War of 1812.

The settlement grew on shipbuilding and river trade. It was the county seat from 1822 to 1868 and gained a railroad in 1859. The seat later moved to Bowling Green, where courthouse construction began in November 1893. Along the way, a cholera epidemic in 1854 killed more than 100 people, and the early settlers of Orleans had to relocate to higher ground after floods.

The area lies near the center of the Twelve Mile Square Reservation, land the Odawa ceded to the United States in 1795, and the 1817 Treaty of Fort Meigs ended their claim to this stretch of the river. The first plat spanned 1.786 square miles. Today the city measures 11.51 square miles by the 2010 count, so most houses stand on land added long after that plat.

The median Perrysburg owner-occupied home is valued at $329,700, and the median household earns $111,643. Just under two thirds of homes are lived in by their owners, so a sizeable share of the housing is rented.

Companies headquartered in the city include Owens-Illinois, a global glass container maker, Burkett Restaurant Equipment and Universal Tube and Rollform Equipment. Levis Commons is the best-known place to shop and eat.

Perrysburg Schools operate a preschool, four elementary schools, an intermediate school, a junior high and Perrysburg High School. Saint Rose School and The Islamic School of Greater Toledo also serve families, and the Way Public Library covers the Perrysburg area.

Education levels run high locally. Among residents 25 and older, 57.6% hold at least a bachelor's degree, and the commute averages 18.9 minutes.

Who approves permits for a Perrysburg house: the city or Wood County?

Both. The City of Perrysburg grants zoning permits, and it contracts with Wood County Building Inspection for building permits, with the zoning permit coming first. The Planning and Zoning Division enforces codified ordinance Chapters 1210 through 1460 and also handles code enforcement, Board of Zoning Appeals applications and Historic Landmarks Commission cases.

The division's published answers help a seller who is closing out old projects:

  • Any change in a fence's height, style or location needs a permit.
  • Each new shed needs one, including a freestanding unit not fixed to the ground, and it must sit at least 5 feet off the lot line and 10 feet from the house.
  • Trailers and recreational vehicles may stay in a front or side yard between April 1 and October 31, on a hard surface at least 5 feet from any lot line.
  • City staff do not survey lots, so use a certified surveyor to find boundaries.

Zoning questions go to the office at 201 W Indiana Avenue, phone 419-872-8060. Building permit questions go to Wood County Building Inspection at 419-354-9190 on weekdays between 7:30 and 3:30, or toll free at 866-860-4140.

Landlords carry an extra obligation. Rental owners in Perrysburg must file a net profit income tax return on rental income and report tenants who move in or out.

How do Wood County deed filing and tax bills work for a Perrysburg seller?

After closing, the deed visits the Wood County Auditor before it reaches the recorder. Under Ohio Revised Code 322.02, any county transfer tax is paid by the grantor to the auditor when the deed is delivered, ahead of recording, and section 319.202 requires the buyer to submit a statement of value. The auditor answers at 419-354-9150 or 866-860-4140.

The Wood County Treasurer collects real estate tax in two installments, due in February and July. About eighty taxing districts exist in the county, each with its own rate, so a Perrysburg bill reflects the levies at that address. Payments go by mail to the treasurer at 1 Courthouse Square in Bowling Green or to participating banks, several with Perrysburg branches, until close of business on the due date, and mailed payments must be postmarked by then. After the due date a 5 percent penalty applies for the first 10 days, rising to 10 percent after that, as Ohio Revised Code 323.13 sets out.

Ohio's property disclosure statute, section 5302.30, tells you to hand buyers the state form promptly. It asks about the water supply, the sewer system, the roof and foundation, and defects you know of. Fiduciary transfers from an estate and inherited houses that you did not occupy in the past year are exempt.

When does a cash purchase suit a Perrysburg owner?

Cash suits cases where timing or condition outweighs the final dollar: an inherited Perrysburg house nobody will renovate, a tenant-occupied rental, or a move for work on a short schedule. The buyer purchases the house with its flaws, so you skip contractors, showings and appraisal waits.

Ask for the offer in writing and set it beside a realistic listing result after commission, repairs and carrying costs. Find out who pays the transfer charges, which date closes the sale, and what happens if the buyer finds a defect. Declining an offer does not stop you from listing.

Who issues a building permit for a Perrysburg house?

Wood County Building Inspection, after the City of Perrysburg has issued a zoning permit. The zoning permit must be obtained before the building permit is released.

Does swapping out a fence in Perrysburg need a permit?

A permit is required any time a fence changes in height, style or location. For a replacement identical in height, style and position, confirm with Planning and Zoning at 419-872-8060 before starting.

When do Wood County tax bills come due?

In February and July each year. Pay late and a 5 percent penalty applies during the first 10 days, then 10 percent.

Do Perrysburg landlords owe the city income tax on rent?

Yes. The city asks owners of rental property to file a net profit income tax return for rental income and to report tenants who occupy or leave their units.

Which disclosures apply when I sell a Perrysburg home?

The state form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 applies, covering the water supply, sewer system, structure, hazardous materials and known defects, delivered to buyers promptly.

What is it like to sell a house in Athens, Ohio?

Selling here means selling in a university town, and Ohio University sets the tone for most deals. Athens is the county seat, 65 miles southeast of Columbus on the Hocking River, and the university, chartered in 1804, is the top employer in Athens County.

The place became a village in 1811 and a city in 1912, once the 1910 census showed more than 5,000 residents. Census estimates put Athens at 25,313 people for 2025, compared with 23,821 in April 2020. Houses range from student rentals and investor duplexes to a smaller group of owner-occupied homes on the hillsides above the river valley.

Three things decide how a quick sale goes: who is likely to buy, what the city expects of the property, and what Ohio asks of you on paper. The sections below cover each one.

How does Ohio University shape the Athens housing market?

The university pulls the market toward renting. In the 2020 to 2024 Census data, only 32.6% of Athens homes are owner-occupied, which sits well below the 71.8% to 88.3% range the same table shows for Beavercreek, Avon Lake and Avon. The city has 7,238 households at 2.30 people each, a median rent of $1,011 and a median home value of $247,000.

  • Many buyers of older Athens houses are landlords who plan to rent to students and staff.
  • Families tend to look near the five Athens City School District buildings: East Elementary, Morrison Gordon Elementary, The Plains Intermediate, the middle school and the high school.
  • Faculty and staff at the Heritage College of Osteopathic Medicine add another group of local buyers.

A buyer who plans to rent the house takes on the rental rules described next.

What does the rental permit program mean if you sell an Athens house?

Athens City Code Title 29 requires a valid permit on every residential rental. The code enforcement office reports more than 5,300 registered rental units, with health and safety inspections each year, run by four officers on a monthly schedule that the city posts online.

A tenant-occupied house brings that permit and inspection record into the sale. Call the Code Enforcement and Community Development office (28 Curran Drive, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.) and ask whether the permit follows the house or must be reissued to the buyer.

The same office registers contractors each year and takes complaints about grass, trash, parking and zoning. Clear any open complaint on a vacant house before you list it.

Does flooding along the Hocking River affect a sale in Athens?

It can, since large parts of the city and the campus sit in the river's floodplain. The city names the Hocking River, Margaret Creek and Coates Run as its main flood sources, and its hazard plan ranks river flooding first among natural hazards, with flash flooding third.

The record is long. Wikipedia lists notable floods in 1832, 1873, 1907, 1937, 1949, 1964 and 1968, and a 1969 Army Corps of Engineers project moved the channel south of town. Athens sits in unglaciated hill country, with ridges about 300 feet above the valley floor. NOAA normals put yearly precipitation near 41.6 inches and snow near 17.6 inches.

Building, filling or otherwise developing in the floodplain takes a city permit, and FEMA maps are linked from the floodplain page. Ohio also gives owners some tax relief after a loss. Under ORC 323.17, a county board of revision may push a payment date back by up to a year when fire, flood or another event destroys at least 25% of a parcel's assessed value (and at least $2,000 of taxable value).

Which local offices handle the common steps of an Athens sale?

Two offices carry most of the load: the city's code enforcement department for property rules, and the county auditor for the deed. The table shows where to start.

What paperwork does Ohio require from an Athens seller?

A seller of a house with up to four units must complete the state's property disclosure form and give it to the buyer as soon as practicable, under ORC 5302.30. It asks about the water supply, sewer, roof, foundation, hazardous materials and any defects you know of. Estate fiduciaries, sellers deeding to a spouse or lineal relative, and sales to a buyer who has already lived there a year are listed exceptions.

  • A buyer handed the form after signing may cancel in writing within three business days.
  • A buyer who is never given the form may cancel too, up to the earlier of 30 days after acceptance or closing.
  • The deed needs the seller's signature, acknowledged before a notary or another official named in ORC 5301.01.

The deed goes through the Athens County Auditor before it is recorded. Ask the auditor's office which transfer and conveyance fees apply, since a title company builds them into the closing statement.

How are property taxes handled when an Athens house sells?

The county bills the tax. According to the Athens County Auditor, bills are typically due in March and August, with exact dates set each year by the treasurer. Ask the Athens County Treasurer for the dates on your parcel before you pick a closing day, so the title company prorates the right amount.

Two reductions may appear on your bill. Homestead covers owners aged 65 or older, owners who are permanently and totally disabled, and surviving spouses of recipients who were at least 59 at death. The Owner Occupancy Tax Reduction covers the owner's principal residence as of January 1 of the filing year.

When does a cash offer make sense for an Athens house?

A cash offer fits when speed or condition outweighs the last few thousand dollars. A listing in Athens means showings, a buyer's inspection and a lender's appraisal, and each can delay closing or bring repair requests.

Direct buyers typically purchase as is. That helps with a rented duplex that has an open inspection item, a house with flood damage, or an inherited property nobody wants to fix. Get at least two offers, ask who pays closing costs, and see the purchase contract and settlement statement before you sign.

More questions about Athens, OH

Can I sell my Athens house while tenants live in it?

Yes. Ohio does not bar the sale of a rented house, and the lease usually carries over to the new owner. Since Athens requires a Title 29 permit and yearly inspections, ask the code enforcement office what a buyer must do to keep the permit in good standing.

Do I have to hand over a disclosure form in Athens?

Usually. ORC 5302.30 applies to homes with one to four units, with exceptions such as estate transfers and transfers to relatives. A buyer who receives the form late has three business days to cancel in writing.

Is my Athens house in a floodplain?

Check the FEMA maps linked on the city's floodplain page, or call the code enforcement office at 28 Curran Drive. Flood risk follows the Hocking River, Margaret Creek and Coates Run, and development in the floodplain needs a permit.

Who records the deed after an Athens sale?

The county recorder files it after the county auditor processes the transfer. ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent against a later buyer with no knowledge of it, so closing agents record promptly.

What if I owe the city for cutting my grass?

Pay it before closing. Athens sends a 5 day notice for grass over eight inches, hires a vendor if the owner does not cut it, and passes unpaid bills to the county auditor to be recorded as a tax lien.

  • The county holds roughly 230,000 parcels, so quote your parcel number on every form.

What is the process for disputing a Centerville property value?

The Montgomery County Board of Revision opens its filing period on January 1 and closes it at the end of March. Each complaint must state the value you want and your reasoning. Under Revised Code 5715.19 the date can run later when first-half collection closes after March 31.

The person who files must prove the case. The county lists acceptable evidence as a sale of the property within three years, a recent appraisal, sales of similar nearby homes, a realtor's market analysis, and itemized repair estimates. Lists of other properties' assessed values, comments on neighbors' upkeep, and tax rate complaints do not count.

Tax year 2025 hearings ran by video or phone and lasted 10 to 20 minutes per property. The board mails a decision within 90 days. Either side then has 30 days to go to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas. A changed value holds until the next countywide update, which comes every three years unless the property is rebuilt or damaged.

What does Ohio's condition disclosure form require of a Centerville seller?

Revised Code 5302.30 asks sellers of buildings of up to four dwellings to describe the water supply, sewage system, roof, foundation, walls, floors, and known hazards on a state form. A buyer who first receives it after signing the contract can back out within three business days.

Transfers by an estate fiduciary, between spouses, to a lineal relative, or by an heir who did not live in the home the previous year are exempt. Centerville is prone to tornadoes, floods, and severe storms according to Wikipedia, so tell a buyer about any storm or water damage you know of.

What is the story behind Centerville's schools and old houses?

Centerville schools enrolled about 550 students in 1863 and stayed in the hundreds until 1955, when the count passed 1,100. By 1969 more than 6,800 students attended, and the district took the name Centerville City Schools that year. Elementary buildings date from 1955 through 2007, among them Weller, Stingley, Driscoll, Normandy, Cline, and John Hole, and the three middle schools are Magsig, Watts, and Tower Heights.

The town also has an Underground Railroad past. Wikipedia reports evidence of four safe houses in Centerville and Washington Township. The Town Hall Theatre was built in 1908 as the township hall and became a performing arts center in 1989. In 2008 voters considered a merger commission with Washington Township, which passed in the city and failed in the township.

Which schools, hospitals, and amenities draw buyers to Centerville?

In all, the district operates two primary schools, six elementary schools, three middle schools, one high school, and an alternative high school. The Washington-Centerville Public Library lists more than 380,000 items.

Miami Valley Hospital South opened in 2007 as an outpatient site with an emergency department and grew into a full hospital with 60 beds by 2013, on a campus beside Interstate 675. Wikipedia calls it the city's largest employer and lists retail and health care as the top job categories. The council-manager government has a seven-member council elected at large, and the Town Hall Theatre downtown dates to 1908. For 2022 the Census shows retail sales of $44,802 per resident.

More questions about Centerville, OH

Which county handles my Centerville sale?

Mostly Montgomery County, with a small portion of the city in Greene County. The county on your deed and tax bill has the auditor, treasurer, and recorder who process your paperwork.

Does a historic stone house in Centerville need a review before I sell?

Ask the city's planning and zoning office whether your address falls in a historic area with review rules. Settle that question before offering a buyer exterior changes.

Who bears the transfer fee on a Centerville house?

The seller. It lands on the seller under Revised Code 319.202, and the closing statement itemizes it.

When can Montgomery County owners file a value complaint?

Filing opens on New Year's Day and closes March 31. Upload your market value evidence to the county portal ten days or more ahead of the hearing.

Do I fill out the disclosure form for an inherited Centerville house?

Often not. The disclosure statute, Revised Code 5302.30, excludes estate fiduciaries and heirs who never occupied the home in the prior year. If you lived there, complete it. Your closing agent can say which case fits you.

Zanesville at a glance

What should you know before selling a house in Zanesville, Ohio?

Zanesville is the Muskingum County seat, built where the Licking River meets the Muskingum River about 52 miles east of Columbus. The 2025 Census estimate of 25,138 people is a 1.4% rise over the 24,783 in the 2020 estimates base, which follows decades of loss from a 1950 peak of 40,517.

The city is named for Ebenezer Zane, whose pioneer trail crossed the Muskingum here, and it served as Ohio's second state capital from 1810 to 1812. The National Road, now U.S. 40, runs through town alongside Interstate 70, and U.S. 22 and state routes 60 and 93 also pass through. The three-way Y-Bridge over the river junction is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Zanesville was once known for pottery. Weller, Roseville and J. B. Owens operated here in the first half of the twentieth century, drawing on local clay deposits. The city peaked economically in the 1950s, and Wikipedia describes its present economy as having relatively high poverty and low labor force participation.

What do the Census figures say about the Zanesville housing market?

Renters outnumber owners here. QuickFacts reports 43.8% owner occupancy for 2020 to 2024, the lowest of the four cities, alongside a $123,700 median home value and $821 median gross rent.

  • There are 10,601 households averaging 2.28 people.
  • Households earn a median $43,280, and 24.1% of residents live below the poverty line.
  • Bachelor's degrees reach 15.1% of adults, and 85.4% finished high school.
  • Commutes average 22.8 minutes each way.
  • Health care and social assistance took in about $1.01 billion in 2022, and retailers sold about $907 million, which works out to $36,876 per resident, the top figure of the four.

With fewer than half of homes occupied by owners, tenants are part of many sales. If your house has a tenant, tell buyers whether the lease runs past closing and who holds the deposit.

Which schools, colleges and hospitals serve Zanesville?

Most students inside the city limits attend Zanesville City Schools, with Zanesville High School as the high school. A few northern pockets of the city belong to the West Muskingum and Tri-Valley local districts, so check which district serves your parcel before advertising it. Private options include Bishop Rosecrans High School and Zanesville Christian School.

Higher education is local. Ohio University Zanesville is a branch campus of Ohio University, and Zane State College sits next to it. Muskingum University is in nearby New Concord. In 2016 the Good Samaritan and Bethesda campuses merged to form Genesis Hospital, and Good Samaritan was closed and demolished.

How does Zanesville's building and code enforcement office affect a sale?

The city's Building and Code Enforcement office, at 401 Market Street, Room 227, enforces the International Property Maintenance Code, the city's codified ordinances and the zoning code, and it can start legal proceedings against violators. Weekday hours run 7:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 740-617-4890.

The office also issues and inspects the permits a buyer's inspector will ask about:

  • Residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, which do not include plumbing.
  • Residential and commercial sidewalk, curb and curb cut permits.
  • Demolition permits.
  • Permits to move a house or an accessory structure wider than 14 feet or larger than 450 square feet.
  • Certificates of occupancy.

The office keeps lists of condemned properties and posts a 2026 annual vacant property form among its code enforcement forms. If your house is vacant, ask the office whether the form applies before you list it. For zoning questions, the county auditor's page lists the city's Planning and Zoning office at 740-617-4909. South Zanesville has its own permit department at 740-454-0492, which matters if your address is just outside the city line.

How do Muskingum County values, appeals and homestead rules work?

The Muskingum County Auditor works from the courthouse at 401 Main Street, takes calls at (740) 455-7109 and keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. The auditor explains that the January 2026 tax bills reflect values set in January 2025, and that an addition, a demolition or newly passed levies can change a bill.

A three-member Board of Revision (auditor, treasurer and commissioners' president, or their designees) adjusts values and has no say over tax dollars. A complaint is a legal filing, lodged with the auditor from January 1 to March 31. The auditor's page warns that a filing is generally limited to once per three years and that withdrawing one uses up the turn. Points that help a seller:

  • Proof is on you, and the outcome can be a higher value, a lower one or none at all.
  • Certified mail brings the hearing notice at least ten days before the date.
  • After a filing, an appraiser from the auditor may visit and propose a settlement figure. Accepting it in writing cancels the hearing.
  • A corporation should have an attorney file for it.

The auditor's brochure for tax year 2025 explains the Homestead Exemption for seniors, disabled owners and surviving spouses. It prints a $29,000 reduction in taxable market value, an income limit of $41,000 that is adjusted annually for inflation, a December 31 filing deadline, and a larger reduction for disabled veterans equal to the tax on up to $58,000 of market value. A seller who receives the exemption should ask the auditor how a sale affects it on that parcel.

Which offices handle common steps in a Zanesville sale?

Most steps involve the city's code office and the county auditor. The table shows where each begins.

Zanesville sale tasks and the office to contact
TaskOfficeContact printed on the page
Permits, condemned lists, code enforcementCity Building and Code Enforcement401 Market Street, Room 227; 740-617-4890
Zoning questionsCity Planning and Zoning740-617-4909
Value complaintMuskingum County Board of Revision, through the auditorFiled January 1 to March 31; (740) 455-7109
Homestead applicationMuskingum County AuditorDecember 31 deadline; 401 Main Street
Address just outside the city lineSouth Zanesville Permit Department740-454-0492

What must a Zanesville seller tell the buyer?

Ohio Revised Code 5302.30 puts a state form in the hands of every one to four unit seller. Fill it in honestly and deliver it promptly. A seller is not liable for an inaccuracy that was outside the seller's actual knowledge, though a buyer given the form late can walk away within three business days.

Gather permit numbers and any notices from the code office before showings, so the buyer sees them with the form.

When does a cash offer make sense for a Zanesville house?

Consider a cash offer for a rental with tenant trouble, an inherited house or a place whose repairs would worry a lender's appraiser. It can also end the monthly cost of a vacant house that keeps drawing taxes and utility bills.

Collect more than one written offer, compare closing costs and closing dates, and ask the title company for the settlement statement a day or two before you sign.

More questions about Zanesville, OH

Who do I call about zoning in Zanesville?

Phone the city's Planning and Zoning office at 740-617-4909. The county auditor's zoning page lists that number next to separate contacts for South Zanesville and several townships, since zoning follows the address.

How often can I appeal my Muskingum County property value?

Once in each three-year period, as a rule. The auditor receives complaints from January 1 until March 31, and one that is later withdrawn still counts as your filing.

Can the Board of Revision raise my value?

Yes, the auditor's page says the board may go up, go down or leave the number alone, and that the burden is on the owner. Bring a recent sale, an appraisal or repair estimates.

Does a vacant Zanesville house need to be registered?

The city's code enforcement page carries an annual vacant property form for 2026. Phone 740-617-4890 to learn whether your address must file before a sale.

What permits might a buyer ask me about in Zanesville?

A buyer's inspector may ask about residential building, electrical and mechanical permits, demolition permits and certificates of occupancy, all issued by the city's Building and Code Enforcement office. Bring permit numbers for any addition or major system replacement.
